entries.section: (1) The growth of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The beginning of the Book of Exodus recalls what the Book of Genesis mentioned at its end (ch. 46): the children of Israel who entered the land of Egypt, seventy souls in number, including Jacob and his sons and grandsons who came from Canaan, in addition to Joseph and his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh (see the commentary on Gen 46:26). Note that they were few, merely a family, but God blessed it and it became a great nation.

entries.section: (1) The growth of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Joseph and his brothers died. Joseph had represented the authority that protected and provided for his family, but in truth it was God who used Joseph. Even after his death, God blessed this family, so they multiplied greatly and became a large people, reaching about 2 million souls, at a time when the population of all Egypt was about 8 million; that is, they became about a quarter of the population of Egypt.
Joseph is a type of Christ: after Joseph's death the number of the children of Israel increased, and by the death of Christ He offered salvation to the many in the whole world who believed in Him.

Trust in God's blessing upon your life, however hard your circumstances may be and however those around you may have wronged you. He strengthens you and makes you grow until those who oppose you fear you, and He gives you grace and respect in the eyes of those around you.

entries.section: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Many years passed after the death of Joseph, during which the Egyptians forgot his services or purposely disregarded them, because of their resentment toward the Hyksos who had ruled them in the days of Joseph, in addition to the nature of human beings, who do not preserve gratitude toward those who served them for a long time. A new king arose who did not care about Joseph and therefore did not care to honor his race, that is, the children of Israel.

entries.section: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Let us deal wisely with them: let us persecute them craftily.
Get them up out of the land: leave Egypt and return to Canaan, so that the Egyptians would lose this labor force that served them.
When this king noticed the tremendous increase of the children of Israel, he considered with his counselors how to stop their growth and weaken them, fearing two things:
1- Their increase in number would make them a force that frightens the Egyptians, so that if enemies attacked them from the east, the children of Israel would join them, fight Egypt and occupy it.

2- Their increase would make them a force that could not be controlled, so that the Egyptians would lose the labor of the children of Israel if they left them and went up to the land of Canaan, where they had been living.

entries.section: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Pithom and Raamses: two cities located near Tanis, that is, Zoan, the capital of Egypt at that time, whose site is now in the Sharqia governorate.
Taskmasters: Egyptian overseers to lead the children of Israel in their work.

The first attempt to weaken the children of Israel and reduce their number was to exhaust them by building cities to store grain, weapons and ammunition near the capital. They worked in forced labor, that is, they received no wages but only their food, and it may have been scanty food, in the hope that some of them would die of exhaustion.

entries.section: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: They were grieved: they were afraid.
Despite the harsh treatment of the children of Israel, God gave them strength and they endured the toil; on the contrary, they reproduced and bore many children, so their strength increased.

God is stronger than all who oppose you, and He mocks them. He permits them to show all their evil toward you, but at the same time He blesses you in the time of affliction, so you become stronger than before, and your heart is filled with a peace that terrifies your enemies.

entries.section: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Because the Egyptians feared the children of Israel, they grew more severe in their treatment of them and exploited them in many exhausting works, the most important of which were:
1- Building cities.
2- Agriculture.

The Hebrews: the descendants of Eber, who was one of the forefathers of Abraham (Gen 11:15); also, since Abraham, the forefather of the children of Israel, had crossed the River Euphrates into Canaan, his descendants are called Hebrews.

The number of Hebrew women giving birth was estimated at tens and even hundreds of thousands; some of them gave birth without anyone's help, while others needed the help of the midwife. There were two famous midwives who were considered the chiefs of the midwives who delivered the Hebrew women, and Pharaoh summoned these two to him.
The stools: in ancient times women gave birth sitting on special stools whose position helped in delivery.

The king commanded the two midwives, together with all the midwives who followed them, that when they delivered the Hebrew women, if the child was a son they should kill him, and if it was a daughter they should let her live; in this way the number of men among the children of Israel would diminish and their strength would gradually weaken.

Although the command came from the king, and although they knew that he sent out spies to make sure his orders were carried out, they feared God more than men, because of their association with the children of Israel, from whom they had learned the fear of God; so they did not kill any male child.

If pressures and temptations multiply upon you to break God's commandments, remember that He is the most important person in your life, so do not anger Him, and trust that when you fear Him He will remove from your heart every fear of all human beings, and will even bless you and protect you.

The king became very angry when he learned from his spies that the newborn male children had not been killed, and he summoned the two midwives and rebuked them for what had happened; perhaps he intended to kill them.

The two midwives answered the king and gave him a plausible reason for the existence of newborn Hebrew male children, namely that the Hebrew women were strong in health and gave birth before the midwife arrived. This is true in many cases, but of course not in all cases, so this is considered a partial lie.
He made them houses: He gave them houses full of good things, and if they were not married, He granted them marriage and happy houses.

Although the two midwives had lied in part, God forgave them and blessed them because they feared Him, and He blessed their two houses. At the same time the people of the children of Israel continued to increase and grow.

Since the king's attempt to kill the males at their birth by means of the midwives had failed, and perhaps he doubted their words but had no proof of it, he resorted to another scheme to weaken the children of Israel, for he gave an extremely cruel command: to throw the newborn male children into the River Nile. By this he would achieve two things:
1- Gradually reducing the number of the men of the children of Israel, so that the people would be weakened.
2- Pleasing the Nile, which they worshiped as a god, by offering it human sacrifices.

But God, who is able to do all things, can preserve His people, and He made the child whom He wanted to live, namely Moses, be drawn out of the water and be brought up in the house of Pharaoh himself, so that he might lead his people and bring them out by the power of God in spite of the king.
Note: in ancient times the word Nile meant the River Nile and all its branches that go out from it and spread throughout the land of Egypt.
The birth of Moses, his upbringing and his flight to the wilderness

While the children of Israel were suffering from the king's cruel command to throw the newborn males into the Nile, a man of the tribe of Levi, Amram, married his father's sister, whose name was Jochebed (this was permitted before the giving of the Law through Moses), and they bore a handsome male child. His mother's heart was attached to him, and she believed in God, who is able to keep him safe (Heb 11:23), so she hid him in her house for three months, exposing herself and her family to being killed by the soldiers who went about the streets to listen for the voices of children and to learn the news of any pregnant woman when she gave birth.
An ark: a basket (a plaited basket). Bulrushes: a plant with broad leaves.
Slime: a kind of pitch (mineral pitch) that helps the bulrush leaves hold together and stick to one another. Flags: a plant with broad leaves that grows on the banks of rivers.

The three-month-old child grew bigger and the sound of his crying rose, so his parents were afraid and were compelled to prepare an ark of bulrush leaves and daub it with slime and pitch to make it a strong ark, and they put the child in it. His sister Miriam, who was thirteen years old, carried him and went with him to the River Nile and placed him on its surface among the flags, and she stood watching where the water would carry the ark. Perhaps her prayers mingled with her tears, like her parents, who had hope that God would save him, and so they did not throw him into the river but put him in an ark.

However hard the affliction is, lift up your prayers and do what is in your hand to do, even if it is small, like preparing this ark, and your God, who is able to do all things, can save you, because your prayers are very precious to Him.

entries.section: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

paragraphs.text: The Egyptian women believed that bathing in the water of the Nile had blessings, and some places in the Nile were set apart for the bathing of great ladies. So one of the princesses, that is, the daughter of Pharaoh, went down to bathe in the Nile with her maidens, and as she was bathing she saw an ark floating on the surface of the water. This was the ark that Miriam had placed, with her brother the child in it. She commanded one of her maids to bring it, and she marveled when she saw a child in it, and said that he must be one of the children of the Hebrews, who throw their male children into the Nile according to her father's command.

entries.section: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

paragraphs.text: Miriam came near the place of the princess to hear what would happen to her brother, and she heard the princess declaring her admiration for the child and her wish to take him for herself and bring him up as her son. At this point God guided Miriam to go forward to the princess and ask her whether she wanted a nurse for the child.

entries.section: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

paragraphs.text: The princess agreed to bring a Hebrew nurse, that is, a mother who had recently given birth to a child, so Miriam went with great joy, told her mother what had happened, and quickly brought her to the princess.

entries.section: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

paragraphs.text: The princess commanded Jochebed, the mother of Moses, to nurse the child in her house and take care of him until he grew and she weaned him, and she promised her suitable wages. This was a declaration of the princess's adoption of Moses, so he became a grandson of Pharaoh.

Do not fear the threats of the wicked, for God saves you from their hands and even subjects them to you, as He subdued Pharaoh through his daughter, saving his son Moses and even paying the expenses of his living while he was in his house with his father and mother.

entries.section: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

paragraphs.text: After the child was weaned, that is, after about two or at most three years, Jochebed brought her son the child to the princess, and she took him as her son by adoption and called his name "Moses", which means drawn out of the water. Jochebed took advantage of the opportunity of having the child with her in the house, and taught him all the spiritual teachings she could; perhaps she also visited him in Pharaoh's palace and was alone with him, as his nurse, to complete his spiritual teaching and fill him with her love.

Take care to teach your children even at a very young age, for they pick up everything that happens around them, even if they are only a few months old. The sight of you praying at home or reading the Holy Bible, or the sight of the prayers in the church ... affects them greatly and is imprinted within them, so that time cannot erase it.

entries.section: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

paragraphs.text: Moses was brought up as a son of Pharaoh in the royal palace for 40 years, during which he learned the greatest sciences of the world, and they cared for his health and physical strength (Acts 7:22-23). His heart was attached to his God and to his people, who were humiliated at the hands of the Egyptians, and he thought of saving them, but unfortunately he relied on his own strength and not on God. As he was walking in the streets of the city, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his brethren, and humiliating him; he became very angry and had pity on his wronged Hebrew brother, and thought of saving him and delivering him from this humiliation.

entries.section: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

paragraphs.text: Moses relied only on his own strength and not on God, and therefore he was afraid ... so he looked this way and that way to make sure that no one saw him, then he fell upon the Egyptian and killed him and buried him in the ground (covered him over), and rescued his Hebrew brother.

The remedy for violence is not violence, nor resisting evil with evil. Ask God to give you wisdom to help others in a sound way, and know that if you become angry and resist evil with evil you will lose your peace and cause those around you to stumble, and you will not stop the one who wronged you from his evil, but will provoke him to wrong you again in a new way. The only one who benefits from all this is Satan, while God, the angels and the saints look at you with sorrow.

entries.section: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

paragraphs.text: The next day Moses continued his attempts to save his people. As he was walking in the streets of the city he saw a Hebrew wronging a Hebrew, one of his brethren, so he reproved the wrongdoer and rebuked him so that he would not wrong his brother.

entries.section: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

paragraphs.text: Moses was surprised that the wrongdoing Hebrew answered him violently and exposed to him what he had done in secret the day before, namely killing the Egyptian, so Moses knew that his secret had been discovered; that is, the Hebrew whom he had rescued the day before had told his loved ones, and what had happened spread among the Jews and then among the Egyptians. The wrongdoer denounced Moses' interference because he was not responsible for settling disputes like the judges, and then accused him of intending to kill him, although Moses had no such intention but was seeking peace and reconciliation among his Hebrew brethren.

entries.section: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

paragraphs.text: The land of Midian: a region lying from the east of the Gulf of Aqaba to the middle of Sinai (Map 1). It was called this after Midian the son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25).

The news of Moses' killing of the Egyptian reached Pharaoh, and he knew that Moses' allegiance was not to him as his father and the one who raised him, but to his Hebrew race, so he commanded that he be arrested and put to death, because he represented a leader of a Hebrew revolt against the Egyptians. When Moses learned of this, he fled very far, from the east of the Delta to the east of Sinai and beyond, which is the land of Midian, and he came to a well, drank, and sat down to rest.
Success built on pride is quickly exposed to ruin, whatever its methods, so be humble and seek God's help before every work.
Map (1) The journey in Sinai (Ex 12 - 19)
The troughs: basins beside the well that are filled with water for the animals to drink from.

In Midian there was a priest called Reuel, which means (God is a friend) (Num 10:29), and his title was Jethro, which means (the exalted or the preferred) (Ex 3:1). He had seven daughters who tended his sheep, and they came as they did every day to water the flock from the well; they drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's sheep.

Some shepherds came to water their flocks, and when they saw the troughs that the daughters of Reuel had filled, they took advantage of the women's weakness and drove them away. Moses was troubled by this injustice, so he stood up against the shepherds and drove them off, and the daughters of Jethro watered their flock. It appears from the verse that this injustice befell them every day, so that they were late in watering their flock. Here Moses' courage, justice and fairness to the wronged are evident, even toward those who had no relation to him.
Defend the wronged as much as you can, and wrong no one, but think of the good of others before your own good, for love does not seek its own.

Because of Moses' help to the young women, they hurried to water their flock, and their father Reuel was surprised at their quick return home. They told their father of Moses' help to them in drawing water and watering the flock, and they knew that he was an Egyptian man, perhaps from his clothes and his language.
Reuel invited Moses to eat a meal with him and welcomed him, and he sensed his chivalry, strength and love; likewise Moses felt at ease in his company and hospitality.
Zipporah: that is, a little bird.

Because the priest of Midian admired Moses, he welcomed him to dwell with him, and Moses also rejoiced to stay with him because of his balance and love, and he even began to help him in tending his flock. When love grew firm between them, and Moses admired one of his daughters, Zipporah, he married her.

Moses had a son whom he named Gershom, which means a stranger, to declare not only his being a stranger in the land of Midian, far from his Hebrew people, but also his being a stranger to the world as a heavenly man. Later another son was born whom he named Eliezer (ch. 18:2-4).

The Egyptians continued to humiliate the children of Israel until the king of Egypt died, who, it seems, had humiliated the children of Israel more severely than others, so they cried out to God to save them from this humiliation, whether by a new merciful king or by any other way.
And God remembered: not because God had forgotten, but He announces the time for fulfilling the promises.

God heard the cry of His people who were humiliated in Egypt and moved to fulfill His promises to His beloved ones, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the forefathers of this people, so that He would save them by His divine power, bring them back to the land of Canaan and give it to them as an inheritance.

God notices, and even suffers with you, in everything you endure, and He is ready to save you and support you if you cry to Him and persist in asking. So trust that you will receive mercy and help and experience His fellowship and power, however long the answer is delayed.
The bush
The back side of the desert: areas of pasture that follow wide areas of desert.

The mountain of God, even to Horeb: Horeb means desert or dry, and Mount Horeb is a range of mountains lying in the south of the Sinai Peninsula. It is called the mountain of God because Moses received the commandments and the Law from its summit. Moses was accustomed to tend the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, and he was eighty years old. One day he led the flock to pasture lands far away in the depths of the desert near Mount Horeb, and he was at that time eighty years old; he had spent forty of them in Pharaoh's palace in Egypt and the next forty in the wilderness of Midian, while the last forty of his life he spent as leader of the people in the wilderness of Sinai until he reached the borders of the land of Canaan; that is, Moses lived 120 years on earth.
The bush: a thorny plant that grows in the desert.

While Moses was tending the flock, he saw a wonderful sight: a flame of fire surrounding a bramble plant without the plant being burned. He marveled at the sight and turned aside with curiosity to learn the truth of the matter.

It says in (v. 2) that the bush burning with fire is an appearance of the angel of the Lord, then it returns in (v. 4) and says that it is the Lord. The word angel means messenger or one sent, and what is meant by the word angel is God sent to us, that is, this is one of the appearances of the Second Hypostasis. Note the repeated appearance of God in the form of fire, as He appeared to Abraham as a burning lamp (Gen 15:17), and after the bush He appeared many times in the form of fire, as in the pillar of fire that led the people in the wilderness (ch. 13:21), and as the fire appeared on the mountain when the commandments and the Law were received (ch. 19:18). The bush burning with fire is a symbol of:
(1) The people of God; the thorns signify the evils of the world that surround them, while the fire signifies God, who dwells in the midst of His people and around them to protect them and save them.
(2) The Incarnation, that is, the union of divinity with humanity, that is, the fire with the bush.
(3) The Virgin, who carried in her womb the fire of divinity: the bush signifies her womb, and Christ is signified by the fire.
Moses heard a voice calling him by name; he marveled greatly and answered the voice without knowing who was speaking to him.

The voice said to him, put off your shoes, for the ground surrounding the bush is holy ground. The taking off of the shoes signifies the holiness of the place, as we do today when we approach the sanctuary, for the following reasons:
1- The shoe is made of the skins of dead animals, so whoever draws near to God leaves behind the perishing material things, that is, detaches himself from them, in order to be occupied with God.

2- The skins from which the shoes are made signify the skins with which Adam and Eve were clothed, so we take them off in order to put on Christ the Redeemer, who justifies us, because the animal sacrifices were a symbol of Christ, who was sacrificed for us on the Cross.
3- The leather of shoes is what drums are made of, so taking off the shoe means leaving superficial, outward worship and caring for spiritual depth.

4- The kinsman is the nearest person to the dead man, who marries his widow to raise up offspring for the dead man; and if he is not willing to marry her, he takes off his shoe so that the kinsman next to him in relationship may marry her. Taking off the shoe in this case means that this kinsman is not worthy to marry the woman, but the kinsman after him is. So whoever takes off his shoes declares that he is not worthy to be the good shepherd of souls, but that Christ is, and that he is merely a servant to Him.

Come forward with reverence when you enter the church, so that you may feel the presence of God, for He is present in it and reveals Himself to the believers in Him who fear Him and reject their evils by repentance in order to meet Him ... He wants to reveal Himself to you and make you feel His presence according to your readiness and your care for Him.

entries.section: (2) The call of Moses to service

paragraphs.text: The One who spoke declared Himself to be God, the God of the fathers of the Hebrew people, so Moses was afraid of the greatness and awesomeness of God and covered his face. This is a declaration that the believers have passed alive to God, and that He even calls Himself their God when He said that He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. This is a clear answer to the Sadducees and to everyone who denies the resurrection of the dead and their life after death (Lk 20:27, 28).

entries.section: (2) The call of Moses to service

paragraphs.text: God showed His fatherhood and His sharing in the suffering of His people in Egypt because of the humiliation they endured from the Egyptians. What is beautiful is that He calls them my people, that is, my own; He declares His fatherhood and His responsibility for them, and despite their many sins He hears their prayers and answers them.

entries.section: (2) The call of Moses to service

paragraphs.text: I am come down: a figurative expression that shows God's condescension and His care to save His people, His hearing and His answering their prayers.

To bring them up: because the land of Canaan is higher in geographical level than the land of Egypt, and the land of Canaan represents freedom, settled life and the worship of God, while Egypt represents slavery and humiliation. That is, to bring them up from humiliation and slavery to a better life.

A good land and a large: fertile and big, for it extends from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the River Euphrates in the east, and from the Taurus Mountains in the north to the Arabian Peninsula in the south.
Milk and honey: rich and sweet foods that signify abundant good: the milk from the abundance of pastures and the honey from the abundance of plants.

God promises to save His people from the hands of the mighty Egyptians and to bring them out to dwell in the land of Canaan, which is a fertile land whose fertility is expressed by saying that it flows with milk and honey, and He will drive out its inhabitants because of their evils and their abandoning of His worship. God makes clear the names of the peoples whose land He will give to the Jews.

It is evident from this that God's condescension to save His people and bring them up is like the condescension of Christ in His Incarnation, by which He saved us from our sins in order to bring us up to heaven.

entries.section: (2) The call of Moses to service

paragraphs.text: God repeats His sense of the distress of His people, and for this reason He decided to send Moses to lead His people and bring them out of the land of Egypt.

Trust in the power of God that is with you, however great or difficult the responsibility may be, because it is God who will work in you to face the powers of the world, and He is stronger than all. So ask for His help, then thank Him for what He has done.

Moses failed when he relied on his own strength to save his people, so he fled to the wilderness and lived 40 years in which he felt his weakness before the power of God, the God of heaven, while he was merely a shepherd. Therefore, when God called him from the bush to meet Pharaoh and lead the people, he made excuses because of his weakness.

It is good to know your weakness when undertaking the service of God; then He supports you with His grace and you can do all things, because by your humility you let God work freely in you, and you glorify Him.

God strengthened Moses by saying "I will be with you", then gave him a sign to strengthen him, namely that they would come out of the land of Egypt and worship God in the wilderness of Sinai, that is, on this very mountain beside the bush.

Moses placed a new obstacle in the way of carrying out his mission, namely that he did not know the name of God, the God of the fathers, as peoples know the names of their pagan gods, especially as they were living among many names of gods of the Egyptians; so he asked God about His name, which he would declare to his people.
Ehyeh: I am He, or I will be; and the meaning of Ehyeh asher Ehyeh is I will be who I will be.

God declared that His name is Ehyeh, that is, I am He, and the meaning of the name is that I am the only God, I am the Existing One, and all other than I is nothing. And He commanded Moses to declare this name of His to the children of Israel.

entries.section: (4) How the children of Israel would come out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Jehovah: that is, the Existing One whose existence is necessary.
God told Moses that the first step in bringing out the children of Israel is to meet their elders, that is, the heads of their tribes and clans, and to declare two things to them:
1- That the name of God is Jehovah Ehyeh, which means, as we said, I am He.

2- That He is the God of their fathers, who promised them many descendants and the inheritance of the land of Canaan, so that they may be assured that He is the God whom they know, who heard their cry and will save them.

And He commanded him to tell them of God's concern for them and His hearing of their prayers, and that He would save them from the slavery and humiliation of Egypt, bring them out of it, and settle them in the land of Canaan in the place of its wicked peoples.

God hears your prayer and feels your need however long the time may be, and He visits you at the proper time, and He is stronger than all the surrounding circumstances. So be reassured and take courage, because He is with you, and as long as He is with you, you are stronger than all.

entries.section: (4) How the children of Israel would come out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: The second step in bringing out the children of Israel is the entering of Moses and the elders of Israel to meet Pharaoh and declare three matters to him:
(1) That the God of the Hebrews has appeared to them.

(2) The request for the children of Israel to go out of Egypt and journey three days into the wilderness to offer worship to their God. This was a modest request in which he did not ask Pharaoh for material things, nor that they should depart from Egypt and not return to it; it is merely worship of the God of Israel, as the Egyptians worship their gods. Even so, Pharaoh refused, which shows the hardness of his heart in refusing this modest request.

(3) They would offer animal sacrifices to please their God, which signify the sacrifice of Christ. These sacrifices are sacred to the Egyptians, so if the children of Israel slaughtered them before the Egyptians' eyes they would provoke their anger; therefore they asked to go far away to sacrifice to their God. This is a logical request that takes the feelings of the Egyptians into account, and even so Pharaoh refused because of his hardness.

entries.section: (4) How the children of Israel would come out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: God told Moses that Pharaoh would refuse his request, so that Moses would not be disturbed, and He declared to him the third step in bringing them out, which is that God would perform many miracles, namely the ten plagues, that would frighten the Egyptians so that they would be compelled to obey God and let His people go.

entries.section: (4) How the children of Israel would come out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: Her that sojourneth in her house: that is, the woman who lodges with her.
You shall put them upon your sons, and upon your daughters: that is, your sons and your daughters shall wear them, and the males in this age sometimes wore gold and silver.

He commanded him that when they went out of Egypt they should ask the Egyptians for gold, silver and clothing, and God would give them favor in their eyes so that they would give them much, because of their fear of their God who struck them with the ten plagues. In this way God returns to the children of Israel something of their rights that the Egyptians had taken away by enslaving them and putting them to forced labor.

This command is not theft, because it is God who commands it. It is a symbol of the spiritual person who believes in God: when God accepts his repentance and saves him from his sins, He gives him many spoils, which are his abilities and gifts that were enslaved to sin, so he is set free and lives with them with God.
The continuation of the dialogue with God

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: Moses expected that the elders of his people would not believe him, so he asked God what he should do.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: God asked him what was in his hand, and he said it was a rod. This was not because God did not know, but so that Moses would be certain that it was a rod, so that the miracle would appear afterward by its turning into a serpent.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: God commanded Moses to cast the rod on the ground, and it became a serpent, so Moses was afraid and ran away from it, for the Holy Bible to confirm that it was a real serpent, so that the turning of the rod into a serpent was a clear miracle.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: Moses obeyed God and took hold of the serpent by its tail, and it became a rod in his hand. The turning of the serpent into a rod declares:
1- The authority of God over nature and all creatures, so that He changes each of them into the other.
2- The authority of the believer over Satan, who is signified by the serpent, and over the various animals and creatures by the power of God.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: By this sign the elders of Israel will believe that the God of the fathers has appeared to Moses, and in this He answered his question and his perplexity that he mentioned in (v. 1). This is the first miracle.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: The second miracle is that Moses put his hand inside his garment and then took it out, and it was leprous, that is, shining white like snow, and then he put it back inside his garment, and it returned as it was, like the rest of the color of his body. This miracle shows God's ability to bring sickness and to heal from it, especially the disease of leprosy, from which none but God can heal.

entries.section: (1) The miracles of God given to Moses

paragraphs.text: God gave him a third miracle, which was to take some water from the river and pour it on the ground, and it would become blood. This signifies the blood of Christ the Redeemer, which changes our hearts, weak as water, into life, whose symbol is blood. These three miracles prove to the children of Israel that Moses has met God, and they are also a confirmation of Moses' faith.

God gives you grace in the eyes of people so that they may know that you are with God. So do not care about the opinion of people, because God will give you grace in their eyes, but only obey Him and declare His voice.
Neither heretofore, nor since: that is, throughout his past life.
Nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: since God appeared to Moses in the bush.

Moses' humility is shown in his excuse for not leading the people, and his argument is his weakness in speech throughout his life; he may have had some difficulty in pronouncing certain letters, being, for example, a lisper. His feeling now is entirely different from his feeling when he left the palace 40 years ago to save his people, when he was relying on his own strength; now he feels his weakness and declares it before God.

Declare your weakness before God before any work or any service or speech, and you will receive grace and strength from Him to succeed in everything, and even to be distinguished from those around you, and God will be glorified in you.

God reassured Moses that He is the Creator of man and of the tongue, and likewise He permits any incapacity in human beings and is also able to complete it. Therefore He is able to complete Moses and support him in his mission however great his weakness or incapacity.

Because of Moses' strong sense of his weakness, he repeated his excuse and asked God to send another in his place. This was a mistaken exaggeration on Moses' part; he ought to have obeyed God since He had reassured him.
Do not make excuses for any service that God places before you, and trust in His power that supports you after you have revealed your weakness to God.

Despite Moses' mistake, God accepted his excuse and strengthened him with a person who would be with him and speak as an official spokesman in his name, namely his brother Aaron, who would go out, by God's guidance, to meet Moses when he returned from Midian to Egypt, and would rejoice at meeting him. But he would be merely a spokesman for Moses, while Moses would be the leader and head over him. Then He reminded him to take the rod with him, with which he would perform the miracles. Aaron later caused problems for Moses by making the golden calf when Moses went up to receive the tablets of the Law on the mountain; would that he had listened to God's word and obeyed and trusted in Him and had not persisted in his excuse.

Note that God reminded him to take the rod, which is a small tool, but with it God would perform great miracles, so that the glory would be to God and not to the tool, just as God uses weak people to be glorified in them, namely His prophets and His messengers, and as He also uses simple natural materials such as water and oil for the Holy Spirit to dwell in them and give the Holy Sacraments to those who believe in Him in the Church.
Do not be stubborn with God, but obey Him quickly so as not to cause problems for yourself.
Moses asked leave of his father-in-law Jethro to return and save his people in Egypt, and he gave him leave. Of course this means that he took his wife and his sons with him.

Here the reason for Moses' strength in his decision to return to Egypt is shown: God had already reassured him that Pharaoh and his counselors who had wanted to kill him long ago were dead, and He commanded him to go to the elders of Israel and then to the new Pharaoh.

Moses set out with his wife and his sons, and they rode on donkeys, and he took with him his rod, which God had commanded him to take with him in order to perform many miracles with it, and then he traveled to Egypt. This rod is a symbol of the wood of the Cross.

God commanded Moses to perform the three miracles with the elders of Israel so that they would believe that it was God who had sent him to them, and then to perform them also before Pharaoh to convince him of the power of God that was with him. And God warned Moses that Pharaoh would harden his heart and refuse to believe in God and submit to Moses, so he should not be disturbed by this refusal. Note that God does not harden anyone's heart toward evil, but He leaves a person to his evil if he insists on it.

When God warns us that there are afflictions on the way of the Kingdom, He wants us not to be disturbed by them when we meet them and to trust in His power that supports us; indeed, out of His love He turns them to our good so that they become steps for us that raise us up to heaven.

God told Moses the end of the dialogue that would take place between him and Pharaoh after he had struck him with nine plagues, namely His saying to him in the end that God commands you to let the people of Israel go, my firstborn son, because it is the only people that believes in Him at that time, while the rest of the peoples, his brothers, will believe later at the Incarnation of Christ. And because Pharaoh would be stubborn in releasing the Israelite people, the firstborn son of God, God would kill his firstborn together with the firstborn of all the Egyptians, and this is what happened in the tenth plague, so Pharaoh submitted and let the people go.
Do not resist God by rejecting His commandments, lest He punish you, and if He punishes you, repent quickly and He will forgive you and you will find your place in eternity.

While Moses was traveling, he rested on the way at a lodging place prepared on the road like an inn, called the inn. There God appeared to him and rebuked him for neglecting to circumcise his son; perhaps in this he had been led by the feelings of his wife Zipporah in her fear and pity for the child. In order that God might show him the seriousness of neglecting obedience to His commands, He attacked him to kill him, perhaps in the form of an angel; and this threat was also to frighten Zipporah, that her neglect could lead to the death of her husband, especially since God had been long-suffering toward Moses, for He appeared to him in the bush and spoke with him in the wilderness and in Midian and charged him with leading the people, and all these were opportunities for him to pay attention to obeying God and to circumcise his son.

Do not be careless in obeying God's commandments, relying on His love and long-suffering, because if He is perfect in His tenderness, He is also perfect in His justice, and by your disobedience you expose yourself to destruction. Let the fear of God be always before your eyes, and you will live in assurance and be made fit to know God and enjoy fellowship with Him.
A sharp stone: a serrated piece of flint used as a knife.

Zipporah remembered her sin in preventing her husband from circumcising his son, out of her fear for him from this surgical operation, and she had not believed in the importance of obeying God's commandment; but when she saw her husband exposed to death she hurried to correct her mistake by performing the circumcision on her son. Then she took the piece of skin stained with blood and touched Moses' feet, her husband's, with it, and said to him "a bloody husband art thou to me", that is, I believe that I am married to you and I circumcise my children, and I believe that the blood saves me from every sin as you taught me; for she declares that by circumcising her son she regained Moses, who was about to die at the hand of the angel, as a husband and bridegroom to her, and regained him by the blood shed through circumcision, which signifies the blood of Christ.

The angel left Moses after the circumcision was completed, and Zipporah confirmed her words that Moses was a bloody husband to her, that is, that her marriage and her family depend on the blood shed in circumcision, which signifies the blood of Christ the Redeemer.
God informed Aaron that Moses was returning to Egypt and commanded him to meet him, so he went out to him and kissed him and rejoiced at meeting him after 40 years of separation.

Moses told Aaron of his meeting with God, who appeared to him in the bush, and of all the conversation that took place between them and the miracles that He gave him to perform in order to bring his people out of Egypt.

Moses and Aaron gathered the elders of Israel, and Aaron, as spokesman for Moses, told them of God's appearance to his brother and the conversation that took place between them, and then Moses performed the miracles before them to confirm God's appearance to him.

The elders of Israel rejoiced and worshiped God, declaring their faith in Him and their submission to Moses. Of course the news spread among the people of Israel, and they rejoiced that God had answered their prayers.

Trust that God hears your prayers with care, and if He delays in answering, it is in order to increase your faith and save you from many sins and show His care for you at the proper time. So persevere in your prayers however long the time, confident of His love, and be faithful in your spiritual striving and in fulfilling your duties, for He will never leave you. The Book of Genesis. The meeting with Pharaoh and his punishing of the children of Israel

entries.section: (1) Moses asks for the release of the people

paragraphs.text: With faith and courage Moses carried out the word of God, and he went in with Aaron to Pharaoh, and they asked him to let the people of Israel go to hold a feast to God in the wilderness and offer worship to Him. There are many opinions about the time of the exodus of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt and about the Pharaoh who was reigning at that time; most likely he was Rameses II, which means that their exodus was in the late thirteenth century BC.

entries.section: (1) Moses asks for the release of the people

paragraphs.text: With pride Pharaoh refused their words, despising the God of whom Moses was speaking.

entries.section: (1) Moses asks for the release of the people

paragraphs.text: Moses repeated his request, making clear that God had met him in the desert and had asked him to lead His people Israel on a three days' journey into the wilderness to worship Him there. He made clear the ability of this God to punish whoever opposes Him, for He could strike the people with pestilence or expose them to the attack of enemies and death by the sword.

entries.section: (1) Moses asks for the release of the people

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh accused Moses and Aaron of occupying the children of Israel with these strange ideas, which led to the disruption of work, and he rebuked them for that and commanded them to go to work and not be occupied with these strange ideas. But in rebuking them he commanded them to go to their burdens, and this is a clear admission from him that he was a tyrant and hard-hearted and put heavy works upon the children of Israel.

entries.section: (1) Moses asks for the release of the people

paragraphs.text: The people of the land: the children of Israel.

Pharaoh marveled at the request of Moses and Aaron, because despite the hard labor the children of Israel were doing, their number had greatly increased; how much more, then, if they rested from work, their numbers would increase and they would multiply more and more.

Do not be troubled if people object to your care for the worship of God or His service or to your encouraging others.. Bear with them and do not argue with them much, and hold fast to God, who rewards you and blesses your life.

entries.section: (2) The burden of work is made heavier on the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Taskmasters of the people: the Egyptian chiefs responsible on behalf of Pharaoh for the forced labor of the children of Israel.

Their officers: the Jewish chiefs responsible for leading the people in the work under the taskmasters. Pharaoh gathered the Egyptians responsible for employing the children of Israel and asked them not to give them straw to make bricks of mud, that is, raw bricks with which they build cities, but to let them go themselves to gather the straw from anywhere in Egypt. This of course required of the children of Israel greater effort and a longer time in the work.

entries.section: (2) The burden of work is made heavier on the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh also required the children of Israel to make the same quantity of bricks that they made every day to build the cities with. This was a punishment for them for trying to rest from work on the pretext of going out to worship God, accusing Moses and Aaron of spreading false words of no use, namely going out to worship God.

Do not be harsh in your treatment of others if they do not agree with you in your ideas, and do not hurry to judge them and condemn them, because God, who is stronger than all, watches you and will punish you if you persist in your harshness.

entries.section: (2) The burden of work is made heavier on the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The Egyptian chiefs responsible for employing the children of Israel carried out Pharaoh's word and commanded them to gather the straw themselves and make the same quantity of mud bricks that was required of them every day.

entries.section: (3) The children of Israel plead with Pharaoh

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel went out to look for stubble everywhere in Egypt to gather it so that they could make mud bricks with it, and their Egyptian chiefs urged them on to gather quickly and to work continuously so that they would make the same quantity required every day as was their custom.

entries.section: (3) The children of Israel plead with Pharaoh

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel were exerting great effort in making the quantities of mud bricks required of them every day, so when the gathering of straw was added to them as well, it became impossible to accomplish all this work. Pharaoh's cruelty appeared when the Egyptian taskmasters gathered the chiefs of the children of Israel and rebuked them for not completing what was required of them, and even beat them severely to frighten and humiliate them so that they would be harsh on their brethren to complete the enormous work required of them, even if it was beyond their strength or some of them fell dead from exhaustion; in this way Pharaoh would reduce their growing numbers.

entries.section: (3) The children of Israel plead with Pharaoh

paragraphs.text: Thy people: the Egyptian taskmasters.

The chiefs of the children of Israel went to Pharaoh pleading with him to lift from them this harsh ruling of gathering the straw or stubble needed to make mud bricks while still being bound to make the same quantity required of them every day, and they entreated him because they had done all they could and still were not able to complete what was required, and the Egyptian taskmasters beat them although they were wronged.

entries.section: (3) The children of Israel plead with Pharaoh

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh rejected the pleadings of the chiefs of the children of Israel and accused them of laziness, and that was why they asked him to go out to worship God, to escape completing their work. And he confirmed his decision that they should gather the stubble and make the same quantity of bricks.
Do not plead with the wicked, because they will not take pity on you, but plead with God, and He will have mercy on you and forgive you, whatever your sins or weaknesses or shortcomings.

entries.section: (4) The children of Israel murmur against Moses

paragraphs.text: The chiefs of the children of Israel went out from Pharaoh in great distress after he had treated them harshly, and they found Moses and Aaron meeting them on the road, and they rebuked them severely for suggesting going out to worship God in the wilderness, the matter they had asked of Pharaoh, and because of which this injustice of gathering straw had come upon them; for this decision would lead to the death of many from exhaustion, so it would be like a sword by which many die.

entries.section: (4) The children of Israel murmur against Moses

paragraphs.text: Moses hurried to God and presented to Him the problem of his people, and even reproached Him because He had not delivered them but the injustice upon them had increased.
Place your problems before God, however difficult they are, confident of His love and His ability to do all things. God's speaking with Moses

God encouraged Moses that Pharaoh's opposition was temporary and would end, and that he would let the people of God go, and indeed would drive them out, that is, send them out quickly. This is what he did after the plague on the firstborn, when he was afraid and wanted to be rid of them because of his fear of their God.

God is able to change the hearts of the wicked so that they submit to you and do the will of God, so do not be disturbed by their threats or their wrongs, for they are temporary, and pray for them that they may return to God.

He declared that He is God, known to the fathers as the Lord Almighty. And here He adds to Moses His new name Jehovah, that is, the Existing One, and none other exists from eternity. The name Jehovah had been alluded to before, but not with such clarity (Gen 21:33). The Book of Genesis
He reminded Moses that He had promised them the inheritance of the land of Canaan and its possession, as mentioned in (Gen 12:2, 26:
1-5, 46:3, 4), all this to remind him of His power and His promises so that his heart would be reassured in the face of Pharaoh's opposition and harshness.
I have remembered my covenant: I will fulfill my covenant, or the time has come to fulfill the covenant.
His tenderness is shown in hearing the prayers and the suffering of His people, as is His justice, since He sees the cruelty of the Egyptians and punishes them.

God is long-suffering toward those who wrong you, so do not doubt His tenderness, for He will surely save you; He is touched by all your pains and will not remain silent over the injustice that befalls you.

He asked him to proclaim to the children of Israel that God would save them with a mighty hand from the injustice of the Egyptians and their enslavement. This is the first mention of the word salvation, which was said here for deliverance from the slavery of Egypt and signifies deliverance from the slavery of sin by the redemption of Christ.
He declares His special fatherhood to His people; He is their own God and they are His beloved children.

And this declaration of His to the children of Israel that they were His people was because of their faith in Him at that time, while the rest of the peoples worshiped idols. This was a preparation for establishing a people who believe in Christ the Savior in the fullness of time, namely the Christians who believe in Him from all the countries of the world, while those of the Jews and the Gentiles who rejected Christ are not His people.

Enjoy the boldness of sonship and remind God of His promises when you need Him, and keep yourself pure so as to be a son worthy of God, and you will receive not only His rescue of you from afflictions but also the fellowship of His love, and you will become as if you were in heaven.
Which I did lift up my hand: that is, I swore.
I will give it you: I promised Abraham and his descendants its inheritance.

He confirmed to Moses His earlier promise to the fathers to give the land of Canaan as an inheritance to His people Israel if they remained firm in faith in Him and walked according to His commandments.

Moses spoke to the children of Israel all the words of God after his heart was comforted and strengthened by these divine promises, but the children of Israel did not have the faith that Moses had, so they did not believe him because of the humiliation they were enduring and the brokenness of their souls.

Beware lest the cares of the world keep you from hearing the voice of God, for they are temporary, and your God is able to reveal Himself in your life in the midst of afflictions. So do not give up your prayers and your readings, but seek God with persistence, and He will save you and lift your cares from you.

God commanded Moses to go in to Pharaoh a second time and ask him to let the people of God go to worship Him. This time he is not to ask permission for a journey of three days, but that they go out beyond the borders of Egypt.

Moses marveled at God's command, since the chiefs of his people had not listened to him and had not believed what he said, so how would Pharaoh accept his word. This was not from weakness of his faith in God for convincing Pharaoh, but from his sense of his personal weakness, that he was deficient and weak in expression and speech; so he attributed the children of Israel's not accepting his word to his weakness, and likewise expected Pharaoh to reject this word because he was of uncircumcised lips, that is, deficient in expression. And because the circumcised is a complete man, a son of God, while the uncircumcised signifies the distant, weak Gentiles, because of his weakness in speech he called himself of uncircumcised lips.
And gave them a charge: He strengthened them with words to say to the children of Israel and to Pharaoh.

God continued encouraging Moses and commanded him to go again to the children of Israel and assure them that God would save them, then go in to Pharaoh and demand of him the release of the people of God, and He gave him the words to say. The Book of Genesis

God is ready to give you a mouth and wisdom that will convince those who hear you, so ask Him, whatever your weakness, and He will strengthen you, and do not fear, however harsh or strong those you will meet may be, because your God is stronger than everyone in the world.

entries.section: (3) The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: He mentioned the sons of Reuben and Simeon, who became chiefs of the clans. He began the sequence from the firstborn Reuben in order to reach Levi, who is the one meant, because he is the great-grandfather of Moses and Aaron. He mentioned the first three sons, who fell into grave sins: Reuben committed adultery with his father's wife during his father's lifetime, and Simeon and Levi killed the tribe of Hamor and Shechem. Here God shows His love in accepting sinners if they repent, for all of them are His children and He loves them despite their sins.

entries.section: (3) The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: He mentioned the sons of Levi and their clans until he reached the mention of Amram, the father of Moses, who was one of the sons of Kohath. He makes clear that Levi, then his son Kohath, and after him his son Amram, lived long lives compared with those around them, to declare God's blessing upon them as a preparation for His great blessing upon their grandson Moses.

entries.section: (3) The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: He declared the marriage of Amram to his father's sister Jochebed, which was permitted before the Law of Moses but was forbidden by the Law afterward (Lev 20:19). And he mentioned the children of Amram, Moses and Aaron, and did not mention here their sister Miriam because the discourse is about Moses and Aaron, who would lead the people.

entries.section: (3) The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: He took care to mention the marriage of Aaron because he would be the high priest, and he married, though of the tribe of Levi, a wife from the tribe of Judah, the tribe from which Christ would come. He also mentioned a great person, Phinehas the son of Eleazar, the grandson of Aaron, who was filled with zeal and killed the man who committed adultery with a foreign woman in violation of the Law of God (Num 25).

entries.section: (3) The genealogy of Moses and Aaron

paragraphs.text: He makes clear that all the preceding genealogies were meant for Moses and Aaron, who would lead the people.

Take care of your lineage to God and the Church in which you were born through Baptism, for this is the source of your strength, and always remember that you are a child of God and His image, so you will walk in what pleases Him and reject the sin that angers Him, and you will be a light to the world and the salt of the earth.
A god: a lord and ruler.
Thy prophet: one speaking what you command him.

God granted Moses awesomeness in Pharaoh's sight through the strength of his personality and the plagues with which he would strike him, so that Pharaoh feared him and submitted and pleaded with him to save him, but unfortunately, because of the hardness of his heart, he would return and refuse to obey God.

God is able to give you awesomeness in the eyes of those around you, even if they object to you or oppose you, yet they feel a strange power in you, which is the power of God. So do not be disturbed by their wrongs, for they result from their anxiety and turmoil. Be strong and hold fast to God's commandments so that you declare His voice through your conduct and your words.

God commanded Moses to speak His words to Aaron, and Aaron to declare these words to Pharaoh. Thus Moses is humbled because he is unable to speak with Pharaoh, and Aaron is humbled because he is merely a spokesman of what Moses commands him.
Accept your incapacity, because it is the means of your salvation through humility before God and cooperation with those around you.

God declared to Moses that Pharaoh would refuse to hear his word, and God would allow the hardness of his heart and even use it to show His wonders by means of the ten plagues, so that the Egyptians would see the helplessness of their gods, that perhaps they might believe, and the children of Israel would be strengthened in the faith that their God is the God of gods.
That I may lay my hand: which calls me to punish and strike Egypt with many plagues.
Great judgments: I will judge them and pass sentence upon them and punish them with great plagues.

God declares His care for Israel, calling them His armies and His people, and therefore they are assured of His care and His deliverance of them from the humiliation and slavery of the Egyptians, so He strikes them to deliver His people from their hands.

God's purpose in the ten plagues is to call the Egyptians to faith, and not only to strengthen the faith of the children of Israel or of Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron believed the word of God and declared their readiness to carry out this word, and they were advanced in age, for they were over eighty years old.

entries.section: (2) Moses' rod swallows up the rods of the magicians

paragraphs.text: Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and told him to let Israel go to worship God in the wilderness as God had commanded them, and he did not refuse their word outright, for Moses was given awesomeness. And Pharaoh asked him for a miracle to be sure that God had appeared to him. God had already instructed Moses to do the miracle of turning the rod into a serpent, so Moses cast down the rod, which is also called Aaron's rod, since Moses used to give his rod to Aaron to do the miracles with it, and it was also called "the rod of God" (ch. 4:20).

The rod signifies the Cross; as it accompanied Moses throughout his life, so also the Cross accompanies us throughout our lives, and by it we receive salvation through the sacraments of the Church. And the rod turned into a serpent because it signifies wisdom, the mother of virtues, by which we know our way to the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Moses' rod swallows up the rods of the magicians

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh brought his magicians, who were led by two great magicians, "Jannes and Jambres"
(2 Tim 3:8). They did in like manner with their enchantments and cast down their rods, and they became serpents.

What the magicians did is the confusion and deception that the devil works on those who do not hold fast to the Church, showing powers and works that resemble the works of God, but by God's wisdom they are easily exposed.

entries.section: (2) Moses' rod swallows up the rods of the magicians

paragraphs.text: The authority of God over Satan appeared when Aaron's rod swallowed up the rods of the magicians, that is, the serpent that came from Aaron's rod swallowed up the serpents of the magicians.

The power of God overcomes Satan in the end, so do not be disturbed by the powers of the world, and be patient until you see the power of God overcome and triumph in you, first by leaving sin, then He lifts the affliction and turns it into blessings in a way that surpasses understanding.

entries.section: (2) Moses' rod swallows up the rods of the magicians

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh refused to believe in the power of God, the God of Moses, and also refused to let the children of Israel go from Egypt, because of his pride.

When God declares His voice to you, do not be stubborn with Him, led by the thoughts of your mind or your emotions, but regret what you have done and declare your apology to God and to those around you; in this you become strong because you are able to face yourself and return to the truth.

entries.section: (3) Preparation for the plague of the river

paragraphs.text: God asked Moses to go the next morning to meet Pharaoh, who goes out to the River Nile; this going out may have been for a stroll, or for bathing, or for a religious festival. And He asked him to rebuke him for not letting the people of God go. Here God begins to show His authority through His prophet Moses, rebuking the wicked that perhaps they might repent. With this the ten plagues begin, by which God intended many benefits, the most important of which are:
1- Showing the power of God, which is exalted above all the pagan gods spread in Egypt.
2- God's support of the truth, His vindication of His wronged children and His punishment of the wrongdoers, that is, Pharaoh and all the Egyptians.
3- Confirming the faith of the children of Israel that they worship the true God, so that they would despise the pagan gods.

4- Confirming the power of His prophet Moses, whom He sent to bring His people out of Egypt, so that Pharaoh and all the Egyptians would fear him and all the children of Israel would also hold him in awe.

5- Shattering the pagan Egyptian gods so that the Egyptians would believe in God and repent and return to Him; and this is indeed what happened, for some of them believed and joined the children of Israel, and they called them the mixed multitude.
There are different divisions of the ten plagues, since they included the pagan Egyptian gods and every power on which the Egyptians depended, and here is this division of the ten plagues:
1- Harmful plagues in which the pagan gods become a source of weariness and distress for the Egyptians, such as turning the river into blood and the plague of frogs, gnats and flies.
2- Plagues of diseases to prick the Egyptians so that they would repent, such as the plague of pestilence on the livestock and the boils on people and beasts.

3- Plagues touching nature, in which God stirred up nature against the Egyptians, so the gods turned into enemies of the people, such as the plague of darkness, when the sun they worshiped disappeared, and the plague of hail accompanied by fire, when the beloved rain turned into hail and fire that killed them.
4- The plague of insects, for He stirred up against them small insects such as the plague of locusts that ate all their good things.
5- Man: and this is the hardest of the plagues, since it killed all the firstborn of Egypt.

If you have tested God through much prayer and the guidance of your father of confession, then carry out what He wants, however difficult, and do not draw back from carrying it out even if it is rebuking some great person or taking an action against the wishes of others.. Be obedient to God before people, and do not fear for yourself their harm or their words, because God will support you.

entries.section: (3) Preparation for the plague of the river

paragraphs.text: He commanded him to threaten Pharaoh that he would strike the River Nile with the rod and it would turn into blood, so that he would know that the God of the Hebrews is God alone and is above all the gods, among which is the River Nile, as the Egyptians worshiped it. The turning of water into blood signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who turns our striving from water to blood, that is, striving to the point of blood. The work of the Holy Spirit is sometimes gentle like water, then grows intense with power to remove every evil from us, even if we endure pains and torments that reach the shedding of blood.

entries.section: (3) Preparation for the plague of the river

paragraphs.text: He also threatened him that the fish would die and stink, and the Egyptians would not be able to drink the water or eat the fish, so they would be deprived of food and drink.
The hardness of your heart deprives you of God's material and spiritual blessings, so take care to obey Him and repent quickly of your sins.

entries.section: (4) Turning the river into blood (the first plague)

paragraphs.text: Their streams: watering channels, that is, water canals.

In vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone: the wooden or stone basins in which water collects. Aaron struck the River Nile before Pharaoh, and all its waters along the length of the land of Egypt, with all the canals and branches going out from it, and also the ponds and all the gatherings of water (pools), turned into blood, so there was blood in all the canals, the streams and the basins for the crops.

entries.section: (4) Turning the river into blood (the first plague)

paragraphs.text: The fish that lived in all the waters of Egypt also died and stank, and the Egyptians were unable to drink water from the Nile or from any of its branches or from the gatherings going out from it, and indeed its stench became troublesome to them.

The Fathers understood from this sign that the water turned into blood for the Egyptians only, while the children of Israel, when they took from the river, had water and not blood, so they drank in peace and did not need to dig wells to look for water as the Egyptians did in (v. 24). What perhaps led them to understand this is that the fourth plague, the plague of flies, was on the Egyptians only and not on the children of Israel (ch. 8:22-24); and likewise the plagues of boils, darkness and the firstborn; so they realized by this that all these ten plagues were on the Egyptians and not on the children of Israel.

entries.section: (4) Turning the river into blood (the first plague)

paragraphs.text: Satan continued his confusion, and the magicians struck with their rods on gatherings of water, and they turned into blood; so Pharaoh refused to believe and submit to God or let his people go.

entries.section: (4) Turning the river into blood (the first plague)

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh remained in his stubbornness as if the plague had not happened, and he neither returned to God nor let his people go.
Do not be stubborn with God and refuse to hear His voice, for every affliction that passes over you is a message from God to you to repent and do a spiritual work with Him.

entries.section: (4) Turning the river into blood (the first plague)

paragraphs.text: The Egyptians were compelled to dig wells to drink from the groundwater, while the children of Israel did not need that, because the water of the Nile remained as it was and did not turn into blood for them. The plagues of frogs, gnats and flies

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: God commanded Moses to teach the people the sanctification of the firstborn son and likewise the firstborn of the beast. These had been killed among the Egyptians by the destroying angel, but the firstborn of God's people were redeemed by the Passover lamb, which is a symbol of Christ, and He purchased them with His blood, so they belong to Him; therefore He asks that they be set apart for Him.
The following is to be noted in the offering of the firstborn:
1- Every firstborn was redeemed by the payment of five shekels of silver.
2- The tribe of the Levites was a redemption for the firstborn of the children of Israel.
3- The firstborn of the children of Israel exceeded the tribe of the Levites by 273 souls, so the redemption of each one was five shekels of silver (Num 3:39-51).
4- The firstborn of clean animals are sacrificed to God, while unclean animals are redeemed with a lamb or have their necks broken (vv. 2, 12, 16).
5- The firstborn remains seven days, nourished by its mother's milk, and then is sacrificed.
6- The owner of the animal takes nothing from these firstborn, such as their wool, nor does he use them for work, but they are offered to God.
7- It is not permitted to vow the firstborn of animals, for they will necessarily be offered according to the Law.

Set apart for God the beginning of your day, your best times and your abilities, in addition to offering the firstfruits of your possessions; and if God chooses one of your children for consecration, encourage him.

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: He reminded them of the day of their departure from Egypt, in which they had been enslaved for more than four hundred years (430 years). It signifies the bondage of sin, since Egypt was full of idols. So He asks them to be committed to eating unleavened bread, which signifies purity, and to reject leaven, which signifies evil, and to sanctify the firstborn and eat the Passover lamb.
When you repent and confess, be more careful to reject the sources of evil, remembering the humiliation of sin, so that you may keep away from everything that leads to it.

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: He reminds them to be committed to the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread throughout their lives, not only in the wilderness but also after they settle in the Promised Land and the pagan peoples are around them, so that they do not care for their foreign ideas but hold fast to the Law of God.

It is understood that the month of Nisan is the month of Abib. The month of Abib was the seventh of the months of the year, but God made it the first month, as mentioned in (ch. 12:2). Thus the Hebrews came to have a civil year, by which political, civil and agricultural matters were reckoned, and another, religious year, which begins with the month of Abib and by which feasts and religious occasions are reckoned. There is a month in the present Coptic year called Abib, but it is different from the month of Abib that existed among the Hebrews. The month of Abib corresponded to the present months of March and April; that is, the departure of the children of Israel was in the spring, which is a suitable time for their journey out of Egypt in the desert.

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: He affirms the commitment to eating unleavened bread for seven days and the removal of leaven, which signifies evil... The number "7" signifies the perfection of the work of the Holy Spirit; that is, we live our whole life in purity, keeping away from evil.

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: "A sign on your hand": that is, you do it with care.
"A memorial between your eyes": you understand it, remember it and see it always, so that you may fulfill it.
"In your mouth": you teach your children by it.
He stresses to him the commitment to observing the Passover and Unleavened Bread throughout his life, and teaching their spiritual meanings to his children through the generations.

Take care to teach your children and loved ones the spiritual teachings, so that they love God and the Church and are bound to Him, and ignorance does not hinder them from God, but the sweetness of fellowship with God is shown, directly or indirectly, according to the circumstances around you.

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: He reminds them to fulfill the law of offering the firstborn to God throughout their lives, when they go out of Egypt and then settle in the land of Canaan, and He commands them as follows:

1- Offering the firstborn of man (the opener of the womb), the male, to God by consecrating him to Him. This is what happened in the consecration of the tribe of Levi for the service of God instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel (Num 3:11).

2- The firstborn of man is redeemed by offering five holy shekels of silver for each firstborn, which is equal to about 75 grams of silver (Num 18:16), and this was before the males of the tribe of the Levites, who became instead of the firstborn of the children of Israel, were counted.
3- Offering the firstborn of the male animal to God as a sacrifice.

4- Unclean animals, such as the donkey, are redeemed by offering a lamb in place of their firstborn, and if it is not offered, the firstborn of the unclean animal is killed so that no one eats it. The Law that Moses received made clear the unclean animals and the clean animals, and it is understood from this, as we mentioned in the Book of Genesis, that clean and unclean animals were known before the Law of Moses; that is, the fathers had learned them from God.
5- The male is offered because he represents strength, for we offer to God the best we have, in addition to the fact that he signifies Christ, who is the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29).

entries.section: (1) The sanctification of the firstborn and the feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread

paragraphs.text: He stresses the importance of teaching the children God's care and His power, which brought His people out with a strong hand from the bondage of Egypt after the killing of their firstborn. The means of their deliverance was the sacrifice of the lamb for the redemption of the firstborn; therefore they redeem the firstborn of man and offer the firstborn of the animals to God. And they place the words of this Law in phylacteries, that is, pieces of leather or cloth fastened on the forehead and wrapped around the head, and they also fasten another on the hand at the forearm. The intention is that they think about this Law and act by it, for the head signifies thought and the hand signifies action.

God did not lead them north to the land of Palestine, that is, the Promised Land, but they went from Rameses, which is near the land of Goshen, to Succoth, and then from Succoth they went south toward the Red Sea. Succoth is on the road between present-day Ismailia and Suez (map 2, p. 93). God made them wander far from the Promised Land because He knew their spiritual weakness: if they faced war they would be afraid and return to the bondage of Egypt. Therefore He allowed them to wander in the wilderness so that their only reliance would be on God. There was a short road leading north to Arish and Rafah, taking about two weeks to reach Palestine, but they would not have been able to face war with the Canaanites because of the weakness of their faith at that time. When they had spent forty years in the wilderness, their faith grew and they were trained in spiritual striving, so they were able to enter the Promised Land and face the Canaanites.
Kill the afflictions that pass over you, for they may be the solution for the salvation of your soul; God knows your nature and keeps you away from evil by using some afflictions.

Joseph felt his estrangement in Egypt despite his great position, and that his bones must be buried in the Promised Land, which is a symbol of the heavenly Jerusalem. So Moses remembered Joseph's command and took his bones with him as he left Egypt, and most likely he also took the bones of Joseph's brothers and carried them to Shechem in Canaan (Acts 7:16).

It is good that you always remember the estrangement of the world, so that you think of the beauty of eternity and strive to attain it, and so care for your readings, your prayers and your repentance.

The son and Israel moved from Succoth to Etham, on the edge of the wilderness of Sinai and on its border (map 2, p. 93). Thus they were left without a helper, and God then showed His care for them and sent them a pillar of cloud that covered them over their heads and protected them from the scorching sun throughout the day. It moved ahead above them, and as they lifted their heads toward it, they walked behind it.

It is a symbol of Baptism, because the cloud is a quantity of water like the water of Baptism, which gives those baptized in it a new nature, guides them to life with God, and passes with them through the afflictions that the scorching sun represents.
And at night the pillar of cloud turned into a pillar of fire from earth to heaven, moving before them, lighting their way, frightening their enemies and protecting them.

Darkness signifies sin and spiritual blindness, which the pillar of fire removes, lighting for them the way of life with God. It is of fire because our God is a consuming fire, and the pillar of fire signifies His commandments, which guide us to life with Him. Let us therefore be cleansed from every sin so that we may be pleasing before Him, and be assured of His power, which protects us from our enemies, the demons.
