The pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire remained with them throughout the days of the wilderness; so God guides us and protects us throughout our life in the wilderness of the world.
Put God before you from the beginning of every day, so that your heart may be at peace and you may fear Him, and so reject sin, meditate on His love and enjoy fellowship with Him.
The crossing of the Red Sea

entries.section: (1) God changes the direction of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: "Pi Hahiroth": it means a farm, and perhaps Pharaoh had a farm there. It is located near the Gulf of Suez.
"Migdol": it means a tower or a fortress, and perhaps Egypt had a garrison in it to defend it against enemies. It is located near the Gulf of Suez.
"Baal Zephon": it means Baal of watching, and perhaps there was a temple there for the god Baal. It is located west of Suez on the Red Sea.
"By the sea": that is, by the Red Sea, at the point from which they crossed the sea.

God commanded Moses that they should turn toward the south, and the pillar of cloud moved to lead the children of Israel not eastward toward the wilderness of Sinai but south, beside the Bitter Lakes, toward the Gulf of Suez. They reached a place beside the Gulf of Suez, that is, before the sea near present-day Suez, most likely about ten miles south of Suez, and the width of the sea there is about eight miles. This distance is enough to hold all the people of Israel and then the army of the Egyptians after them.

entries.section: (1) God changes the direction of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: "The wilderness hath shut them in": they became hemmed in in a dry desert, not knowing where to go, as if they were in a building that had been shut upon them.
News of the movements of the children of Israel will reach Pharaoh through his spies, and he will learn of the change of their course and think that they are bewildered.

entries.section: (1) God changes the direction of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: "I will harden Pharaoh's heart": God uses Pharaoh's pride, so that the king hardens his heart.
Pharaoh and his army will pursue the children of Israel to bring them back to Egypt to serve him, and so the glory of God will be shown in the victory over him.

Do not be troubled by the increasing power of the wicked, for it is temporary, and God will give you victory in the end, because their power is nothing before God. God is long-suffering toward them, that perhaps they may repent, and so that your faith may be established and you may receive more abundant blessings.

entries.section: (2) Pharaoh regrets letting the children of Israel go

paragraphs.text: After the departure of the children of Israel, Pharaoh felt his loss at the disappearance of this great number of workers in his service, and he regretted letting them go. Indeed he wanted to bring them back, and his servants and counselors encouraged him in this.

entries.section: (2) Pharaoh regrets letting the children of Israel go

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh set out with his war chariot and the men of his army to bring back the children of Israel.

entries.section: (2) Pharaoh regrets letting the children of Israel go

paragraphs.text: "Captains over every one of them" (literally, his charioteer soldiers): the soldiers trained to ride in war chariots and to fight the enemies from them.

"Chariot": a vehicle of iron and wood drawn by horses, in which the soldiers ride, so that they can run swiftly. Pharaoh took with him 600 war chariots, the soldiers trained to drive them, and a great army that was distinguished from the armies of the surrounding countries in the whole world.

The number (6) points to the whole perfection of human work, and the number (100) points to the perfection of the work of the community; that is, (600) means the utmost strength of man, especially since Pharaoh was the strongest of the kings of the earth at that time.

It is noted that some of the horses had died in the plague of hail while others lived, because those of the Egyptians who feared God had hidden their cattle, in addition to the purchase of other horses from the neighboring countries to replace what was lost, so that their armies would be complete and ready for war.

entries.section: (2) Pharaoh regrets letting the children of Israel go

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh hurried with his army toward the children of Israel and overtook them while they were before the Red Sea, south of Suez.
If you have kept away from sin, do not return to it through the hardness of your heart, lest this be your last opportunity and you perish in sin.

entries.section: (3) The terror of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: When the children of Israel saw the greatness of the Egyptian army, they were very afraid, so they prayed to God with all their hearts, crying out that He would rescue them from this death or bondage.

entries.section: (3) The terror of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel murmured against Moses because they felt that their destruction before the Egyptians was certain, since they saw the sea before them and the armies of the Egyptians behind them. They were convinced that their death was certain, and they rebuked Moses for not leaving them in the bondage of the Egyptians.
Do not yield to sin, however difficult it may seem; it is better for you to die while striving than to yield to it.

entries.section: (3) The terror of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Moses reassured them that the Lord would fight for them and defeat the Egyptians, and their threats and fear would vanish. He said all this by faith; perhaps God had informed him that he would triumph and be saved from the hand of the Egyptians, who would die, and that no harm would touch him and his people, so he believed the word of God.
By faith you can see what others do not see, and so you live in peace.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: Moses prayed in silence and God heard him; indeed He counted his deep, quiet prayer as a cry, so He reassured him and asked him to bring the people near to the sea.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: He commanded him to strike the sea with the rod so that it would divide into two halves and the children of Israel would cross on dry ground in the midst of the sea.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: He told him of the hardness of Pharaoh's heart, who would not benefit from the miracle of the parting of the sea but would pursue the children of Israel even into the sea. He told him this to reassure him when he saw Pharaoh pursuing them inside the sea, and He commanded him to wait for the power of God, which would triumph over him.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: God's purpose is not only to save His people but also the faith of the Egyptians when they see the defeat of their king and his army and their death.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: It is declared here that the pillar of cloud or the pillar of fire is an angel of God who protects His people. The cloud used to cover the children of Israel to protect them from the heat of the sun, and now it turned into a pillar from earth to heaven separating the people of God from the Egyptians to protect them, so that the Egyptians could not see the people of God because of the mist. This was for the protection of the people of God and a warning to the Egyptians, that they might believe and turn back from pursuing the children of Israel. It is understood from this that the parting of the Red Sea took place in the daytime before the sun set.
Learn from God's warnings, so that you do not persist in your sin but return by repentance, and He will save you.

entries.section: (4) The parting of the Red Sea

paragraphs.text: "The one to the other": the Egyptians to the children of Israel.

The pillar of cloud continued to separate the children of Israel from the Egyptians, and when night fell it turned into a pillar of fire, so the Egyptians were afraid and could not approach or harm the children of Israel.

entries.section: (5) The crossing of the sea by the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Moses struck the sea with the rod, and it divided into two halves by a strong east wind, and the bed of the sea appeared as dry land.
The rod signifies the Cross, which opens a way for you in the midst of the world, that is, the sea, so that you walk in peace.

entries.section: (5) The crossing of the sea by the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel advanced and walked on the ground, with the water like a wall to them on the right and on the left. They trusted in God who protected them, so they were not afraid of the water that stood miraculously like a wall on both sides of them.

entries.section: (5) The crossing of the sea by the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: Because of Pharaoh's hardness, he pursued the children of Israel into the sea and did not repent or learn anything from the miracle. The distance over which the children of Israel walked in the divided sea was about seven miles, at a place south of Suez. This long distance allowed about 2 million people to cross in it, followed by a great, mighty army of the Egyptians.

entries.section: (5) The crossing of the sea by the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: "The morning watch": that is, the time of daybreak, which is the end of the night, because the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea throughout the night, and at its end the pillar of fire moved and drew near to Pharaoh's horses and chariots. The horses were afraid and did not want to advance, so they drove them forward with great difficulty.
"Looked unto the host of the Egyptians": God looked upon them and troubled them with the pillar of fire that drew near to them, and they were very afraid.

"Took off their chariot wheels": the wheels of his strong iron chariots came off, because of the horses drawing back and the soldiers striking them to advance, so the chariots swayed and some of their wheels came off.

When God saw the hardness of Pharaoh's heart, He moved the pillar of fire toward his horsemen and chariots, and his strongest horses were afraid, and some of the army began to feel the power of God that protects His people, so they tried to flee and draw back. But Pharaoh's orders were strict to continue the attack and keep pursuing the children of Israel, and this was the last opportunity God gave them for repentance. It is noted that the Egyptians felt that the God of Israel was very strong and was fighting for His people, so they were troubled, but unfortunately they did not believe with the faith that calls to repentance and turning back; rather, their faith was like the faith of the demons in God, that is, they were insisting on their sin, so they perished. Even if they tried to flee, it was out of panic and fear, but they did not truly believe in God.
Repentance in words is not enough, but it must be carried out with swift striving, because your negligence will bring disgrace upon you.

After the children of Israel had come out of the sea and were in the wilderness, while the whole army of the Egyptians was inside the sea and the pillar of fire was still before them inside the sea, separating them from the children of Israel, God commanded Moses to strike the sea with his rod so that it would return as it was, and it covered the whole army of the Egyptians, and all of them died.
The children of Israel had crossed the sea walking on dry ground and then came out of the sea into the wilderness of Sinai.

In the morning the children of Israel found themselves safe in the wilderness, and then the sea cast up many of the bodies of the Egyptians on the shore, because all of them had died; some of their bodies were on the bottom and some were thrown by the waves onto the shore.
Before the mighty power of God, the faith of His people in Him was established, and they submitted to their great leader in faith, Moses.
Look at God's works with you and meditate on them, so that your faith in Him may be established and you may submit to His commandments. The Tasbeha (praise) and going to Marah and Elim

Moses led the people in praise and glorified God for His great power in His victory over the enemies and the protection of His people, despite the strength of the Egyptian army with its chariots and horsemen, as they all drowned in the sea. This is the first song of praise to the Lord in the Holy Bible, written by Moses, and it speaks of two subjects:
1- God's rescue of His people and the destruction of their enemies (vv. 1-12).
2- A prophecy of their entering Canaan and their victory over its inhabitants (vv. 13-20).
Because of Moses' love for God, he loved praising Him until God became his glorification and his joy, so he blessed Him and declared his faith in Him above all the pagan gods.

The power of God appeared as a warrior greater than all the warriors of the earth, so His name became the greatest of warriors, that is, able to triumph in all wars however strong the enemies may be. This does not contradict His being the God of heaven, because He disciplines the enemies that perhaps they may repent, and if they exhaust all opportunities for repentance, He destroys them, that perhaps whoever sees them may believe and return to God and enjoy His fatherly tenderness and mercy.
The strongest army in the world at that time, the Egyptian army, with its chariots and horses of which it boasts, was drowned.
"The depths": the waves.
The bodies of the enemies sank like a stone to the bottom of the sea, and they became like stone because their hearts were of stone and refused to believe in God.
The right hand represents power, so the power of God is stronger than all the enemies, who signify the demons, and we no longer fear their wars.
God's wrath against the wicked consumes them quickly, and He likened them to stubble in the swiftness of its burning.

"The blast of thy nostrils": He likens God to a man with a nose from which breath goes out, and because God is strong, His breath is very strong; what is meant is the east wind that dried the sea so that the children of Israel crossed over it. "The waters were gathered together": they began to rise one upon another to become like a wall on both sides.
"The floods stood upright": the flowing waters stood upright like a wall on both sides.
"As an heap": the raised hill.
"The depths were congealed": the waves became solid like a dry wall inside the sea.

God sent an east wind that divided the Red Sea, so the waters congealed like a wall on both sides so that the people of God might cross in safety. Thus the power of God that works miracles appears, giving the waters a new nature that is not their own, which is to stand vertically like a wall, and this is against the law of the earth's gravity for liquids. God has done many miracles of this kind, among them His walking, and Peter's, on the water (Mt 14:26, 29).

Pharaoh dared in his wickedness to follow the people of God to seize them and return them as slaves to him in Egypt and to kill whoever opposed him, thinking that he was able to overtake them and bring them back as spoil for himself, they and all that was with them. So Satan dares against the children of God, but they defeat him by the power of God.
God commanded, and the sea returned as it was after the children of Israel had come out, so the Egyptians drowned and became heavy as lead and clung to the earth as if they were earthly and carnal.

God is greater than all the pagan gods in His holiness... praised above all, a worker of miracles that the mind cannot imagine; His servants praise Him with fear, while His enemies tremble and shudder.
God stretched out His hand over the sea and it covered the Egyptians, and the sea swallowed them up and they sank to its bottom.

God rescued His children from the bondage of Egypt and brought them out to the wilderness of Sinai to worship Him in the tabernacle of meeting, where His holy sanctuary is. He guided them by His mercies and His fatherly tenderness, and had compassion on them because of their faith and their sense of their weakness. He redeemed them by bringing them out of the bondage of Egypt by means of the Passover lamb and His killing of the firstborn of Egypt, and He guided them to walk in the wilderness to Mount Sinai, where He declared to them the commandments and the tabernacle of meeting, and they set it up there.
All the nations heard of this miracle, such as the land of Palestine, that is, the land of Canaan, which the children of Israel possessed afterward, and they were very afraid of God and His people.

God gives His children awe in the eyes of others, as they feel a wonderful power in them and fear to wrong them despite their weak appearance, because God protects them and makes their enemies fear them.

He gives examples of the inhabitants of the Promised Land, namely the Edomites, the Moabites and the Canaanites, who were afraid when they heard of the crossing of the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians.
"Thou hast purchased": by Your bringing Your people out of the bondage of Egypt to become a people of Your own.

All the peoples of the earth were afraid and became silent as a stone before the power of God that appeared in His people when they crossed the wilderness of Sinai and entered the Promised Land, and when they crossed the Red Sea by a divine miracle and the strongest army in the world, the army of the Egyptians, died before them. This prophecy was fulfilled by the defeat of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, and Balak king of Moab was troubled by them (Num 21:1-3).

The children of Israel did not come out of the bondage of Egypt to live in the wilderness of Sinai but to possess and be established in the land of Canaan, and to build the temple in Jerusalem on Mount Zion to worship the Lord all their days, and that God might reign over the hearts of His children, and that there might come from them Christ, who reigns forever.

He presents the summary of the miracle, which is the drowning of the whole Egyptian army and the deliverance of the children of Israel, who crossed into the wilderness of Sinai by walking on dry ground in the midst of the sea.
God is able to perform any miracle to rescue and keep His people in every generation, so be at peace and hold fast to your prayers, confident in the power of your God.

"The sister of Aaron": she was called so because Aaron was the older in age, although Moses was more famous than he, and out of Moses' humility he did not attribute his sister to himself but to his brother.

"Timbrels": round frames of wood with a thin skin stretched over one of their faces, with metal discs fixed to them, so that when struck against the wall these discs or small cymbals move and produce a strong sound and clear tones.

"Dances": calm movements offered as worship to God, which were used anciently to express joy and praise to God, as David danced before the ark of the covenant (2 Sam 6:14). This is of course entirely different from worldly dancing, which God hated and because of which Moses destroyed those who danced around the golden calf (ch. 32). The women also took part, led by Miriam the sister of Moses, in praising God, using timbrels as musical instruments to express their joy.
Miriam was leading them in praise like Moses her brother, magnifying and blessing God who triumphed over His enemies.

Because of the importance of this praise that Moses spoke and Miriam his sister followed in it, the Church takes care to repeat it every day in her Tasbeha and calls it the First Hoos, that is, the first praise, because it declares the power of God with His faithful children, which gives them victory over the demons, gives them spiritual blessings and then brings them into heaven.
"Shur": it means a wall, and it lies north of the wilderness of Sinai, and Etham is on its edge, so it is sometimes called the wilderness of Etham, as in (Num 33:6-8) (map 2, p. 93).

After the people had glorified God and rejoiced in freedom, they walked three days in the barren wilderness of Sinai, led by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, that is, God was leading them, until they reached the wilderness of Shur, a barren wilderness with no water or grass.
"Marah": a wilderness whose waters are bitter even now, lying south of the Springs of Moses near the northeastern bank of the Gulf of Suez.
The children of Israel reached a wilderness in which there were springs of water, but it was bitter and could not be drunk because of its bitterness, so they called it Marah.
The people felt great distress, as they almost died of thirst, and they murmured against Moses their leader and against God.
The servant is responsible for those he serves and must bear their murmurings and pray for them, so that God may satisfy them, shepherd them and solve their problems.
"There": in Marah.
"There he made for them a statute and an ordinance": that is, the commandment that God spoke in the next verse.
"And there he proved them": He allowed them the affliction of the bitter water to show their faith in God or their murmuring.

Moses prayed by the power of God, and He answered him and instructed him to cast a tree, or a branch of it, into the bitter water, and it became sweet, and the people drank of it and were satisfied. Thus Moses passed the test successfully because of his faith and his prayer, while the people showed their weakness in their murmuring and lack of faith. And as he cast the tree into the water and it was buried in it and made it sweet, so by the burial of Christ in the tomb He raised us from death and gave us a new, sweet life with Him. The tree signifies the Cross that accomplished our redemption, so we were satisfied with the Holy Spirit, and the placing of the tree in the water signifies the sacrament of Baptism that we received from the blessings of the Cross.

God charged the people through Moses to listen to the commandments of God after they had seen His power for the second time since the miracle of the crossing of the Red Sea, and He asked them to obey Him so that they would not be exposed to the diseases that fell on the Egyptians in the ten plagues, but that God would heal them of every disease they might be exposed to, as He healed the bitter water so that it became sweet.
"Elim": it means trees, and it is a fertile oasis lying southeast of Marah, that is, inside the wilderness of Sinai and not far from the Gulf of Suez.

After the trial of the bitter water, God led them to a fertile region, Elim, in which there were 12 springs of water and which was full of trees, for there were seventy palm trees in it. They signify the twelve tribes and the seventy elders in the Jewish supreme council (the Sanhedrin), and they signify even more the grace of the New Testament, in which there are 12 disciples and 70 apostles.
If you endure the trial, you receive blessings from God that you do not expect, so you are satisfied and refreshed by His grace and rejoice with a true joy.
The manna and the quails

entries.section: (1) The hunger and murmuring of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: "The wilderness of Sin": it is a desert region lying between Elim on the west and the wilderness of Sinai on the east (map 2, p. 93). What is meant by the wilderness of Sinai is the middle part of the wilderness of Sinai extending east of Suez to the borders of the land of Sinai. The wilderness of Sinai mentioned here extends from the middle to near the south of Sinai. The cloud moved from Elim and they reached the wilderness of Sin as they were walking beside the Red Sea, and there was no food in it. The dough with which they had come out of the land of Egypt had run out, so they became hungry. This was in the second month on the fifteenth day, whereas their departure from the land of Egypt was on the fifteenth day of the first month; that is, they reached the wilderness of Sin about a month after their departure.
The details of the journey in the wilderness of Sinai are found in the Book of Numbers (Num 33).

entries.section: (1) The hunger and murmuring of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron instead of praying, trusting in the power of God who had brought them across the sea.

entries.section: (1) The hunger and murmuring of the children of Israel

paragraphs.text: The people spoke to Moses and Aaron and rebuked them for the lack of food and their exposure to death, and they regretted leaving Egypt, remembering the meat and bread they used to eat there and forgetting the humiliation of bondage.
Do not seek the places of sin, however rich they may be or however great their material benefits, and however great your need; death with Christ is better than life in sin.

God answered the people's murmuring with blessings that cannot be imagined: food coming down from heaven in a very huge quantity covering the ground, so that all the people would be satisfied. Moreover, the food coming down from heaven is given daily, so that a man takes of it what suffices him for the one day. By this God tests the people, whether they will believe His word and obey Him, so that no one stores any of this food, or whether they will disobey Him and not be content with the need of the day. God's testing of His people for forty years in the wilderness after their being baptized in the cloud signifies the temptation of Christ for forty days in the wilderness after His Baptism at the hand of John the Baptist, and as the children of Israel entered the Promised Land after crossing the wilderness, so Christ also began His ministry of preaching and drawing souls after His temptation in the wilderness.

"They shall prepare that which they bring in": they make it ready for eating by grinding it and baking it or cooking it in any form (Num 11:8). God commands them to gather on the sixth day enough for two days, so that they may rest on the seventh day and be free for the worship of God.

Moses and Aaron knew that God would give meat in the evening, which is the quails (v. 13), coming in great migrating flocks from Europe to central Africa, passing through the wilderness of Sinai in great weariness and flying close to the ground at a height of about one meter, so that they are easy to catch because they fly slowly. This matter of the quails happened either (1) for one day at the beginning of their entering Sinai and then, years later, for a month in the region of Taberah (Num 11), or (2) their words here are about what would happen later, when they ask for meat and He gives them the quails; the details of this story are mentioned in (Num 11). But in the morning of this day, and throughout the forty years, the manna came down like rain from heaven.

Moses made clear to them that God would give them meat in the evening, which is the quails, and bread, which is the manna, in the morning, and he declared that he was merely a mediator between them and God, who had heard their murmuring and answered with His tenderness and gave them their needs.
Moses and Aaron proclaimed the presence of God and His hearing of the people's murmuring, and asked them to rise and come forward to hear the voice of God.
God is present, but you do not feel His presence unless you draw near to Him in prayer, and then you receive His blessings and He forgives you your sins.

While Aaron was speaking to the people of what God had commanded him and Moses, and announcing to them the coming down of food from heaven, the glory of God appeared in the cloud; that is, a great cloud, attracting attention, appeared.

God spoke from the cloud and the people heard His voice, and perhaps they distinguished the words, or Moses and Aaron did, and told the people that God would give them meat in the evening, which is the quail bird. The flocks of quails came twice: the first time at the beginning of the people's departure into the wilderness, and the second time for a month when they murmured against God because they were weary of the manna, and that was at Taberah. In the morning, God gave them the manna, that is, the bread coming down from heaven.
God is long-suffering toward you and answers your murmurings with blessings, that perhaps you may believe in Him, thank Him and apologize for your murmuring.

entries.section: (3) The coming down of the quails and the manna

paragraphs.text: "Came up": flew at a height of about one meter from the ground (Num 11:31). "Quails": a bird resembling the quail and the size of a dove, but its neck and legs are longer than the neck and legs of a dove.

What God had said was indeed done, as flocks of quails passed in the evening of the same day, and the people took of them as they wished. In the morning the dew, which carries the manna, covered the wilderness around the children of Israel.

entries.section: (3) The coming down of the quails and the manna

paragraphs.text: In the morning the dew evaporated, and the people found a fine thing covering the ground, resembling flakes or brittle frost, and white in color.

entries.section: (3) The coming down of the quails and the manna

paragraphs.text: The people asked about this thing that covered the ground, and Moses said to them, it is the food that God has given you; therefore it was called manna, and because they did not know what it was they said, "Who is it?"
The manna is a symbol of Christ in the following:
1- The manna came down from heaven, as Christ became incarnate and descended from His heaven to live in our midst.
2- The manna is white, as Christ is pure, without sin.
3- The taste of the manna is sweet, like the words of Christ, sweet to the soul.

4- The manna came down after the murmuring of the Jews because they had no food, and it made peace and satisfied them, as Christ by His Incarnation and redemption made reconciliation between God and mankind.

5- The manna came down in the early morning, and the people went out to gather it, or else it melted with the rays of the sun; likewise whoever wants to live with Christ must rise early to Him and put Him before all his worldly concerns.

6- A man gathers of the manna what suffices him for his daily food, just as the Christian must be content in meeting his material needs, not busying himself with storing up or worrying about the future, because he is satisfied with Christ, who satisfies him even if what he has of material things is little.
7- Whoever gathers of the manna more than he needs and keeps it for the next day, it spoils; likewise whoever does not use the means of grace that he knows and the word of God, it condemns him.

8- The people did not know this food, so they said, "Who is it?"; likewise no one can know the essence of Christ, but we know something of His attributes and His relation to us as far as we can understand.
9- They would bake it or cook it, that is, they used fire in cooking it; and Christ also bore sufferings to offer us salvation and spiritual satisfaction.

entries.section: (3) The coming down of the quails and the manna

paragraphs.text: Moses commanded them to take what they needed of this food, and he told them that each one should take the measure of an omer, which equals 2.29 liters, that is, about two and a third liters.

God's gifts may seem strange at first because they are higher than worldly blessings, but when you obey God and thank Him, you discover their sweetness more and more. God's arrangements may seem strange or contrary to your planning, but if you accept them with contentment, you discover in time that they are the best thing for you, and satisfy you, and suit your life and lead you toward God.
Each one gathered as much as he wished of this food; some gathered much and some little.

The surprise appeared when each one measured what he had gathered in order to carry out God's commandment to gather an omer for every person, and they discovered that what they had gathered was an omer for each individual, whether they had gathered much or little.
When God blesses your works, He gives you good enough for you, and even if it seems little, you will be satisfied with it.

Moses commanded them not to leave any of it until the next morning, but some of them doubted the coming down of the manna the next day and kept some of it, but were surprised to find it full of worms and loathsome, not to be eaten, so Moses was angry with them because of the weakness of their faith and their disobedience to God.
The people continued to gather every day what they needed of the manna. The strange thing is that when the sun rose the manna melted and became liquid, and the earth drank it.
If you do not rise early to God to receive His blessing in prayer, the blessing may depart from you and your opportunity be lost, as the manna would melt and be gone.

entries.section: (5) The manna does not come down on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: The people obeyed and gathered on the sixth day twice what they gathered on the other days, because the manna would not come down on the Sabbath. The rulers of the people told Moses what they had done, to make sure that this was the command of the Lord, so that he would not be angry with them as happened when some of them kept some of it until the next day and it bred worms (v. 20).

entries.section: (5) The manna does not come down on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: Moses said to them, cook it so that you may eat of it in the way you wish, and keep the rest until the next day, and it will not spoil, so that you may be free on the seventh day for the worship of God.

Take care of Sunday, the Lord's Day, and increase your prayers and good works, remembering that on this day Christ rose to give you a new life; make it a day distinguished from the rest of your days, so that you may feel God and enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (5) The manna does not come down on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: God's word was indeed fulfilled, that the manna that was kept would not spoil with stench or worms the next day, that is, the Sabbath.

entries.section: (5) The manna does not come down on the Sabbath

paragraphs.text: Moses told them to eat of the manna that was kept on the Sabbath, because no manna would come down on this day; so this became a custom with them, to rest on the seventh day to be free for worship.
Be sure that God provides for your needs, and your being occupied with His worship will not diminish the material blessing but will increase it.

entries.section: (6) The people's disobedience in going out to gather the manna

paragraphs.text: Some of the Jews did not believe God's word and went out to make sure for themselves that there was no manna on the seventh day. This shows their doubt of God's commands and their attachment to material things.

entries.section: (6) The people's disobedience in going out to gather the manna

paragraphs.text: "Abide ye every man in his place": what is meant is that they should not go out in the morning to gather manna but be free on this day for the worship of God, leaving all material work, moving only short distances if necessary, as the elders of the Jews determined.
God reproached the people in His speech with Moses because they had gone out on the Sabbath to gather manna although He had commanded them not to go out, so He rebuked their disobedience.

entries.section: (6) The people's disobedience in going out to gather the manna

paragraphs.text: After this incident the whole people obeyed the word of God and did not move on the Sabbath to gather manna.

entries.section: (6) The people's disobedience in going out to gather the manna

paragraphs.text: He describes the taste of the manna as sweet, like wafers made with honey, and its form as small grains like coriander seed. The Book of Wisdom tells us how every person who ate the manna felt a particular taste as he desired, and this is a wonderful mystery, that the manna had different tastes according to the desire of each one.
Believe the word of the Holy Bible even if it is above your mind, and do not transgress its commandments, so that you may enjoy its blessings and God's pleasure with you.
"A pot": a vessel.
"The testimony": the ark of the covenant in the tabernacle of meeting.

God commanded Moses that they keep a quantity of manna in a vessel, so that throughout history they would remember the miracle of the Lord in feeding them in the wilderness. They kept the manna afterward in a golden vessel inside the ark of the covenant. The quantity of manna that was kept was the measure of an omer, that is, about 2.29 liters.
The keeping of the manna in the golden pot signifies:
1- The Incarnation of Christ, for as the manna came down from heaven, God came down and became incarnate in the fullness of time.
2- The manna signifies Holy Communion from the Body and Blood of Christ.
3- The golden pot signifies the Virgin who carried Christ in her womb.

God continued to send the manna daily to feed His people for 40 years in the wilderness of Sinai until they reached the Promised Land, where they found cultivated land and ate of its fruits, and the manna ceased. Moses said this by the spirit of prophecy, for the manna ceased when Joshua entered the Promised Land and they began to eat the fruits of the land; in addition, it may have ceased for the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, who took possession east of the Jordan in the days of Moses (Num 32, Josh 13).

God's gifts to you continue as long as you feel your need of them, but when you find material things to lean on, God stops His gifts. So do not be distressed by the lack of some resources or the fewness of friends and loved ones, because God Himself compensates you for them, and He is your true strength and your personal friend.
The omer equals, as we mentioned, 2.29 liters, and it is a tenth of a known Jewish measure, the ephah, which equals 22.9 liters.
The symbols of the manna: we note from the above that the manna signifies:
1- The Incarnation of Christ, for He said of Himself, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven" (Jn 6:51).

2- The Body and Blood of Christ, for He said, "the bread that I will give is my flesh" (Jn 6:51). And He also said, "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you" (Jn 6:53).
3- It is the glory that we receive in heaven, for He said, "To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna" (Rev 2:17). The spiritual meanings of the manna:
1- Faith and reliance on God, who provides for our needs daily.

2- Obedience to God, whose commands exceed our mental comprehension: their going out every day to gather the manna, not keeping any of it for the next day except on the sixth day, and not going out on the seventh day.
3- Rising early to God before any work, in prayer and reading His Holy Bible, as they used to rise early before sunrise to gather the manna before it melted in the heat of the sun.
4- The importance of work and spiritual striving, which appeared in their going out every morning to gather it.
5- The blessing of God, for what each person gathered was enough, whether he gathered little or much.

6- God's keeping of our food and our needs, for the manna, which melts in the light rays of the sun in the early morning, remains firm and produces different cakes and baked goods after the women put it on the strong fire (Wis 16:27).

7- The variety of God's blessings to man so that he may delight in them, for the taste of the manna for each one who ate it was according to what he desired, that is, its flavor differed from one person to another according to the liking of each one (Wis 16:25).

8- Contentment, for God gave them one food and did not give them different kinds of foods, and because of their contentment He made His food differ according to the desire of each one. This is what calls the faithful to fasting and detachment, so that God blesses the little they have and it becomes sweet and satisfying to them. The bringing forth of water from the rock and the defeat of Amalek

Since the eighth commandment forbade theft, here God decrees the penalty for the one who steals, which is restitution of four or five times as much, as a kind of discipline for the thief and to show the seriousness of the effect of his theft on others, by bringing fear and disturbance upon them, so that he must compensate them with more than he stole from them. And if the size and price of what was stolen increases, the compensation is greater (five oxen - four sheep). The greater the thief's greed, the greater the discipline he needs, with greater compensation, because the one who steals an ox is bolder in evil than others, besides the fact that he deprived its owners of the price of hiring it out or of using it in work, so the compensation for his theft is greater.

May you think about the effects of your sins on others so that you turn back from them, and then try to make up to others, not only with an apology but with words and deeds of love, so that you restore to them trust in you and peace of mind in dealing with you.

If the thief breaks through the wall or the door during the act of theft, and the owner of the goods senses him, rises to defend himself and strikes the thief so that he dies, the thief deserves this death because of his evil, and the owner of the house is not avenged upon or punished, because he was defending his property.

The sun be risen upon him: the thief continued trying to steal until daybreak, and then the owner of the goods can call to his neighbors and they can seize the thief, so he has no need to kill him in self-defense.
There shall be blood shed for him: that is, he is alive and can be seized alive, and it is not lawful to kill him.

He should make full restitution: the thief is punished by making restitution for what he was trying to steal. Since he had not taken it, slaughtered it or sold it, it says only that he shall make restitution and does not specify the amount of the restitution; this is determined by the judges, and it is usually double. If he have nothing: if he is poor and destitute.

Then he shall be sold for his theft: he is sold as a slave to the owner of the goods or to someone else, and the owner of the goods takes the price; and it is the right of the owner of the goods, if he takes him as a slave, to sell him to whomever he wishes if he does not see fit to keep him with him. This calls for not being hasty in killing the thief, and decrees that he be punished with restitution, and even if he is destitute, he sells himself as a slave to the owner of the goods.

If the thief is caught with the stolen goods in his hand and has not disposed of them by slaughtering or selling them, that is, he has not gone further in his greed and theft, he is disciplined by paying lesser compensation, which is double.

Here he speaks of unintentional theft that results from negligence, in the case of the shepherd who lets his sheep eat from his neighbor's field. Here he must compensate his neighbor with the best fruits of his own field, because he could have kept the sheep away but was merely negligent, that is, he took what was not his, namely the fruits of his brother's field.
If fire break out, and catch in thorns: if thorns or any wood or goods burn in someone's field.

So that the stacks of corn burn: the fire moved with the wind from the burning thorns to the neighbor's storehouses, where he keeps goods piled one upon another, of grain or anything else, and these stores burned. Or the standing corn, or the field: that is, crops that had begun to dry, or any goods that were in the field.

He that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution: the one who lit the fire and did not take care that it should not reach his neighbor is responsible for this negligence, and the judges decide on the appropriate compensation; but it will be less than for the one who was negligent with his sheep eating his neighbor's crops, because keeping sheep away is easier than stopping a fire.

If a man deliver to another silver or goods to keep as a trust for someone else, and it is stolen, and the thief is caught, this thief makes restitution of double only, because the stolen goods were found with him and he had not disposed of them.
If it is impossible to catch the thief, the one who was keeping the trust is brought before the judges to examine whether he stole this trust or it was stolen from him.
The cause of both parties: the one who deposited and the one with whom it was deposited, or the thief and the one robbed.

In the end he decrees the summary of the law of restitution, which is that anything stolen that is found with the thief is compensated for with two, after the judges examine him and decide that he is the thief. That is, if the one with whom the thing was deposited denies the deposited thing and his guilt is proved, he pays double; and the one who found something lost and denied it pays the owner of the lost thing double. And bringing their cause before God means bringing it before the elders so that they may judge who is the thief.

If a man delivers to another a trust such as an animal, and it dies, or is hurt, or is stolen from him, the owner of the animal and the trustee are brought to the court, and if it is proved that the trustee did not interfere, the owner of the animal receives no compensation at all, because he was faithful over the animal.
No man seeing it: there was no witness who saw what happened to the animal.
The oath of the LORD: he raises his right hand and swears by the truth.

If the animal deposited with the trustee is stolen because he was careless in guarding it, he makes restitution for it since it was stolen, because he was negligent in watching over it. But if it was stolen while grazing in the wilderness by some passing traveler without the trustee seeing, he makes no compensation at all, as stated in (v. 10).

If a wild beast attacks the deposited animal and kills it, the trustee presents evidence proving that it was torn, which is the testimony of witnesses or parts of the animal's body that the beast left behind, and this evidence is presented to the court, so the owner of the animal receives no compensation.

If a person borrows anything and it is lost or broken, and the owner of this thing is rich and not in need, he does not compensate him for what was damaged. But if the owner of the thing is in need, the borrower must compensate him.

And if a man hires anything and the thing he hired is lost or broken, he does not compensate its owner, because he paid the hire for this thing, and this hire compensates for any damage that may occur.
Entice: he showed affection for the purpose of fornication.

If a man approaches a virgin and influences her emotionally until he commits fornication with her, he must bear his responsibility, marry her, and pay her father the dowry, the amount customarily paid in such cases according to custom and society, which is fifty shekels of silver (Deut 22:29). It is noted that this amount is more than the usual amount in a dowry because he sinned against a virgin; and if he marries her, he does not divorce her, that is, he is bound to his new marriage. Here he deals with the problem through a positive act, which is marriage.

But if the girl was betrothed and committed fornication with the man of her own will, both are stoned; but if the man raped her, that is, she was the one wronged, the man who assaulted her is stoned alone (Deut 22:23-27).
If a man commits fornication with a virgin and wants to marry her but her father refuses, he is bound to pay the dowry as compensation for his offense against her.

Sorcery is considered dealing with demons and submission to them, and it also draws souls to deal with them; so it is spiritual fornication and a promotion of fornication by causing others to fall. That is, sorcery is a rejection of faith in God and a resort to another power, which is Satan, the adversary of God; therefore the Law commands that sorcerers be put to death. It says "a witch" because most of those who practiced sorcery at that time were women (1 Sam 28:7, Acts 16:16).

The sin of causing others to stumble is a hideous sin, for it makes others fall into evil; so instead of a person striving for good and drawing souls to God, he makes light of them and of their salvation. Therefore be careful in your words and actions so that you do not cause anyone to stumble.

Fornication with animals is not an offense against a human being, but it is uncleanness and immersion in bodily pleasure. This sin was widespread among the Canaanites, among whom the children of Israel lived; therefore whoever does this is put to death, because it is considered uncleanness, it angers God, and it deserves death.

It is understood from this verse that uncleanness is an evil that greatly angers God, even if neither party complains; so if two agree to commit fornication, God is angry at their evil because it is uncleanness.
The worship of idols is spiritual fornication; therefore whoever does it is punished by death.

Do not exploit the stranger, because he knows no one in the place, so that you trouble him or oppress him and demand of him more than his duties; for lack of mercy greatly displeases God. And so that God may stir their feelings of mercy, He reminds them that they were strangers in Egypt for many long years, so that, recalling how hard the feelings of being a stranger are, they may have mercy on strangers.

The widow is the woman without a husband, that is, without support, and the fatherless is the one without a father, that is, without care; and so they always signify the need for mercy. Therefore wronging them is harder than wronging any ordinary person, and is considered a great injustice.

Care for the weak and the needy, have compassion on them, help them and bear with them because of their hard circumstances. And do not forget that you are the widow who has no support but God, and the fatherless who has no true father but God, and the stranger in this world who is poor of every virtue, so that you may be humbled and seek God's mercies, and this will move you to be merciful to everyone.

God declares His fatherhood and care for the weak in His attention to the prayers of the oppressed, such as the widow and the fatherless. If your oppression of the widow and the fatherless increases, He is angry with you, and enemies attack and kill the men, so that your wives become widows and your children fatherless, because you did not have compassion on the widow and the fatherless.

Another form of mercy is lending to the needy. He requires His people not to charge usury, that is, any interest on the amount borrowed, but it is enough that they take back the same amount, sharing with the needy person in the amount of interest they have given up. And of course, if feelings of mercy are stirred, a person can lend and not demand that the other repay what he borrowed; and it is better to help the needy from the beginning with the amount as a gift. Debts were released by their owner when the seventh year came (Deut 15:11-17), and it was permitted for the Jews to take usury from non-Jews (Deut 23:19, 20). But sadly the Jews abandoned this law, as is shown by what happened in the days of Elisha the prophet with the widow woman (2 Kgs 4:1).
Raiment: this is the outer garment that covers his body and keeps him warm during the night if he has no other covering.

If a poor man is compelled to pledge his garment because of his need for money, and walked naked that day and could not repay what he owed within the day, then before the going down of the sun, that is, after he has worked and received his wages and still could not repay, the one who took the garment must return it to him so that he may sleep in it, for how can he sleep naked when he may have no covering? And if he wrongs him and keeps the garment with him, then in his distress and need he cries out to God, and then He hears him, because He is merciful, and takes vengeance on the one who wronged him for exploiting the poor man.

God's mercies toward the needy also appear in what the Law prescribes, that it is not permitted to take a widow's garment in pledge because of her particular circumstances, but she borrows without pledging anything (Deut 24:17).

Another form of oppression is abuse. However troubled a person may be, he must not dare to revile God or the ruler of his people, but must endure, and he will understand afterward the reason for the affliction he is passing through, and perhaps the reason is his sin.
Man goes on and on in the sin of oppression, and is not content with oppressing human beings but dares to oppress God also:

First: by reviling God while murmuring (v. 28). Then, in this verse, by not offering the firstfruits, whether of the grain gathered on the threshing floor, or of the grapes and olives pressed in the winepress, or of the firstborn sons, for whom a ransom is offered, as mentioned in (ch. 13:13).

Likewise God requires them to offer the firstborn of animals such as cattle and sheep, and God's mercy appears in that the animal is taken only after seven days, so that it may suckle from its mother the basic milk that nourishes it, and out of respect for the mother's motherhood toward her suckling; this is compassion for the animal.

Offer the firstfruits and the tithes to receive God's blessing on all your possessions, and know that God does not need your gifts, but they are so that you may show your love for God, your sympathy with the poor and your care for the needs of the Church, and God will repay you with many blessings.
He forbids them to eat an animal torn by beasts, because it is unclean for two reasons:
(1) That it has been touched by an unclean animal, which is the predatory animal.
(2) That its blood did not come out of it but was held in it, so it becomes unclean.
And He commands them to cast it to the dogs. In this He calls them to holiness, not only in eating clean meat but in all their life, so that their hearts may be pure from evil and loving God.
Justice, the feasts, God's presence with them, and refusing to mingle with the wicked

Here He rejects the sin of lying by rejecting false reports, and therefore a person cannot bear false witness, for this is supporting false speech; that is, the Law calls him to reject lying in all its forms.

Do not make light of lying through exaggeration and overstatement or through understatement and belittling, but be careful in all your words and do not be hasty in them, and examine every report you hear, and God will guide you to distinguish truth from falsehood; and do not spread false talk without intending to, leading others astray and angering God.
He also warns against sharing in any evil by word or deed, and against supporting anything false, even if everyone agrees on it.
Do not pity the poor man because of his weak appearance and so pervert justice and wrong the rich man, but be just, and let the poor man be punished if he is in the wrong.

God calls them to help others, not only loved ones and relatives but enemies also. If an animal belonging to one of their enemies strays away from him and is lost and one of the Hebrews finds it, he must take hold of it and bring it back to the enemy. And if this was in the Law of the Old Testament, how much more in the New Testament we must love enemies and have compassion on them.

If your heart is filled with love, you will love every person, even if he wrongs you or is your enemy; for through love you become like Christ, you reach the Kingdom, you put your enemy to shame, and you break the evil that is in you and in him.
Wouldest forbear to help him: you refused to help your enemy.
Thou shalt surely help with him: you must help your enemy.

He gives another example of helping others and chooses an animal, the donkey, which carries loads and belongs to an enemy, and has fallen to the ground on the road under the weight of the load. He requires him to lift the load off the donkey and set it up so that it may continue its way; for lifting such loads is usually not done by one person but by two or more, that is, he helps the one who wrongs him to set his donkey on its feet.

He gives another example of helping others, which is helping the weak, such as the poor man. If he brings a suit before the judges to examine some problem, he must not join the rich in pressing the poor man so that he loses his case because he has no champion on account of his poverty, but must declare the truth and support the poor man and not pervert justice.

In helping others, He calls them to support the innocent and the righteous before the judges, so that he does not lie, that is, bear false witness, and wrong the innocent and kill him and justify the wicked; for God is not pleased with this, because playing with words, that is, lying, can mislead the court so that it wrongs the innocent and justifies the wicked.

Be careful in your words lest you suggest an accusation against the innocent or flatter the wicked because of his position or your embarrassment before him; but proclaim the voice of God gently and clearly even if it does not please the wicked, for God's pleasure with you is more important than people.

He also forbids, in their helping others, bribery, which influences a person to blind him to the truth, so that he looks for crooked ways and loopholes in the law to justify the one who gave him the bribe, and so loses his justice as a judge, since he becomes like a blind man who does not see the truth.

He asks them to help others in the case of strangers who have no support from others, and to remember that they were in need of help when they were strangers in Egypt, from the days of Joseph until Moses.
The Law also commands that the land be sown for six years and then be given rest in the seventh year, for several purposes:
1- The poor eat from it the remains of the crops in it and the natural plants that grow in it.
2- What is left after the poor is eaten by the animals.
3- The land rests from the strain of cultivation to make up for what it has lost and prepare for sowing in the following year, and this is scientifically beneficial.
In addition to the spiritual benefits, which are:
1- Faith in God and reliance on Him, because He promised to give double the harvest in the sixth year, which would suffice their needs for two years.
2- An opportunity to devote themselves to the worship of God in the seventh year.

And when the children of Israel neglected to carry out the commandment of the seventh year, God punished them with captivity, so that by depriving them of their land for seventy years they would make up for what they had neglected in sanctifying the seventh year in the past, before the captivity (2 Chr 36:21).
The stranger: the foreigner who serves you and works for you.

The law of compassion also appears in the law of sanctifying the Sabbath day, for agricultural work is left on the Sabbath, and thus rest is given to the animals working in the cultivation of the land, and likewise to the slaves, in addition to the hired workers he hires from the Gentiles.
Here he summarizes what preceded, confirming the carrying out of the preceding commandments, the most important of which are the worship of God and the rejection of idols.
Here He sets out the three most important feasts of the Jews, which are.

The first feast is the Passover, the cause of their deliverance from the slavery of Egypt, and it is a type of the Lord Christ the crucified Redeemer. And the other two feasts are the harvest and the ingathering; for in the time of material joy we must thank God and glorify Him.
The feasts were mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Num 18, 28).

The Passover is followed by the feast of unleavened bread, free of leaven, which they eat for seven days, and it signifies purity from all evil, which is signified by leaven. And He requires them to offer God's gifts in this feast as proof of their love for Him, and they keep the feast from the evening of the fourteenth day of the month of Abib (Nisan) until the evening of the twenty-first day of it.
And the month of Abib mentioned corresponds to the months of March and April, and it is different from the Abib found in the Coptic year.
Take care to offer something to God every day through worship and doing good, so that you do not stand before Him empty on this day, and on the last day you will find something to offer Him.

The feast of harvest (or the feast of Pentecost): this is the gathering of the crops that ripen at the beginning of the season, which are the winter crops such as wheat. This feast falls fifty days after the first Sunday after the Passover, and this Sunday was called the feast of firstfruits, and it was mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Deut 16). The feast of ingathering (which is the feast of tabernacles): in it the crops that ripen late are gathered, that is, the summer crops such as grapes and olives, and its duration is a week beginning on the fifteenth of the seventh month (Ethanim). The people dwell in booths during this period in remembrance of their sojourning in the wilderness of Sinai, and it was mentioned in detail in (Lev 23, Deut 16). In these two feasts each one offers the firstfruits of what God has gathered, that He may bless the rest of the harvest gathered, and they are to be glad because God allowed them to give to Him, and likewise the needy rejoice, who are satisfied by these gifts.

God redeemed the firstborn of the children of Israel with the Passover lamb from the plague on the firstborn; therefore the males owe their lives to God and come in these feasts to thank Him and praise Him.

And the male represents his family and not only himself, so all the males come to keep the feast to God in these feasts. Of course women can also attend, but at least the males attend as representatives of their families to offer their gifts to God and thank Him because He saved them from slavery in Egypt and from death, just as we now thank God in the feasts because He saved us from the death of sin.

He commands them in the feast of the Passover that the sacrifice be accompanied by unleavened bread without leaven, because unleavened bread signifies the purity with which a person comes forward to receive God's salvation.

He also commands them not to leave any of the Passover sacrifice until the next day, as in (ch. 12); and in general the fat of any sacrifice offered to God is burned on the altar of burnt offering, for it is God's, and neither the priest nor the people eat of it, so the fat must be burned on the altar on the day the animal is slaughtered, that is, the part belonging to God is offered immediately after the sacrifice is slaughtered.
The house of the LORD: the tabernacle of the congregation or the temple of Solomon that was built later.

Here He stresses offering the firstfruits. And God's mercy appears in that they are not to boil a kid newly born that is still suckling from its mother; for God teaches us compassion toward animals so that we may have compassion all the more on our poor and weak brethren. In addition, it is His rejection of a pagan belief among the Gentiles that prescribed cooking a newborn kid in its mother's milk and then pouring out its broth on the fields to give fertility to the land. And in general the Law teaches a person not to cook the small slaughtered animal and eat it with its mother's milk, which was supposed to feed it so that it might live by it, so that he may learn compassion in all his dealings.
An Angel: what is meant by the angel here is a messenger, and he is either:
1- A luminous angel who leads them on the way until the Promised Land.
2- An angel who appears in the form of the pillar of fire or the pillar of cloud.

3- God Himself who speaks with them, and what is meant is the Angel of the Covenant, that is, the Second Hypostasis, in the form of a voice speaking or a cloud appearing in the tabernacle of the congregation, showing His presence and being there.
He warns them so that they may obey this Angel, because he represents God or is God Himself, since He says My name is in him, and he will not pardon their sins if they persist in evil.
He promises them that if they obey the Angel, that is, obey God, He will defend them against their enemies, that is, they will walk in assurance in all their life.

He also promises them that the Angel will bring them to the Promised Land and will destroy the wicked peoples dwelling there so that they may dwell in their place. The destruction was complete or partial for some, that is, a small remnant of them remained according to the greatness of their evils; but God had commanded the destruction of all, yet the children of Israel were negligent in driving them out and killing them after Joshua.
Obedience to God's commandments protects you from the wars of the demons, so however hard they are, do not abandon them, but ask for His help that you may enjoy His care and love.

He also warns them against taking part in the worship of idols worshiped by the Gentiles in whose place they will dwell in the Promised Land, and moreover He asks them to tear down the walls and pillars and temples (their images) that they set up for their worship.
And if some object that killing these peoples involves cruelty, because they had no chance to know God, and what is the fault of their children who are killed, the answer to that is that:
1- God speaks to all human beings through His voice within them, which is the conscience.
2- Nature speaks of the existence of God and His oneness.
3- These peoples had heard of what God did with His people, their crossing of the Red Sea and the ten plagues, and this was enough for them to believe in Him.
4- There are examples of faith and life with God among the Gentiles, such as Rahab the harlot (Josh 2, 6:25) and Ruth.

5- The death of the children was painful to their fathers, that perhaps they might repent, and God, by His foreknowledge, knows that these children would have become wicked. Likewise God will judge the children who did not sin in a way different from the wicked adults.
He stresses to them that they should worship God only, and then God will bless their bread and their water and protect them from diseases and heal them from them if they afflict them.

God's blessing rests upon you if you worship Him and your heart does not cling to the material things of the world; He then provides for your material needs, and you are not hindered by illnesses or the obstacles of the world from worshiping Him, so you live in joy all your days until you reach the Kingdom.

God also promises them, if they hold fast to His worship, to bless every pregnant woman so that her child is not lost, and to give offspring from all the wombs of its women, so there is no barren one, that is, they increase in number and strength. Then He also promises them length of days, confirming the increase of their number.
All the people to whom thou shalt come: the pagan peoples whom you attack and drive out because of their evil.
Turn their backs: they run and flee before you.

God adds also that He appears in His majesty in His war with the enemies, so they fear and flee quickly from before the children of Israel. And the awe of God appears either in the dignity of His children, so that the enemies fear them, or by some other means such as the hornets (v. 28) or thunder.

Hornets: plural of hornet, an insect that gives unbearable stings, which God sends before the children of Israel in their war with the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, so they flee from before them in the war (Josh 24:12, Wis 12:8, 9).

Here appears God's wisdom in driving out the enemies gradually, so that there may be an opportunity for the children of Israel to build up the cities in their place. But if He drove them out quickly, the wild beasts would come and dwell in their abandoned cities and the children of Israel could not enter them; and at the same time, driving out the peoples gradually was an opportunity for these peoples to repent and for some of their individuals at least to return to God (Wis 12:10-27).

Do not be troubled if your striving against any sin lasts long, for God removes it from you gradually so that you do not fall into pride or any other sins, for He knows the fierceness of the devil, and at the same time you have an opportunity for your faith to be established through spiritual striving and to be strengthened by the grace of God.
Another reason for driving out the enemies gradually is to give the children of Israel an opportunity to take care of cultivating the land, so that they eat of its fruits and enjoy them.

God defined for him the area of the Promised Land that he would possess, which extends southward from the Red Sea (the Sea of Suph) to the northwest, which is the Mediterranean Sea, that is, the sea of the Philistines; and from the wilderness, that is, the wilderness of Sinai in the southwest, to the river, which is the river Euphrates in the northeast. This actually happened in the days of David and Solomon (1 Kgs 4:21, 24). But in the New Testament the people of God are those who believe in Christ in every place in the world, and not within the area of a particular land.

He requires him not to make peace or covenant with the inhabitants of the land and dwell with them, but to drive them out, lest if he mingles with them he becomes bound to the worship of idols and leaves God; and this actually happened in the era of the Judges (Judg 2, 3). But whoever of the pagan peoples believes joins the people of God, like Uriah the Hittite and Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 11:3, 24:16). The covenant with God and Moses' ascent of the mountain

entries.section: (1) The call of Moses to go up the mountain

paragraphs.text: Moses went up for the first time when God called him to receive the commandments and the Law (ch. 19). After he heard the Ten Commandments he went down to the people to tell them, and found them trembling at the sight of the smoking mountain (ch. 20:18-20); so he reassured them and went up to hear the ordinances of the Law mentioned in (ch. 21-23). And God calls him again to receive the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation, and this time He calls with him Aaron and his two sons Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, who are as their leaders and judges, and that is because he will receive the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation, which will need the priestly work of Aaron and his sons.

And He asked them to worship afar off, at the foot of the mountain, because of the holiness of the mountain, since God had descended upon it in smoke, mist and fire, so that they might represent the people in submission to God, just as we now bow down in the church before the sanctuary, because Christ dwells in it with His Body and Blood.

Nadab and Abihu: the sons of Aaron, who came forward with their father and their uncle and saw, but who erred afterward by offering strange fire before God, and so died, although their position qualified them to advance in the priesthood and to cleave to God (Lev 10:1).

Seize the opportunity now to be joined to the Church and her sacraments, and if you have an opportunity to serve, do not leave it; and stand firm in humility before God in all His commandments and the teachings of the Church, for negligence was a cause of the destruction of many who were near to God, such as the priests Nadab and Abihu, and Judas Iscariot, the disciple of Christ.

entries.section: (1) The call of Moses to go up the mountain

paragraphs.text: This group leaves the people and draws near to the mountain, but the one who will go up the mountain and come near to God is Moses alone, because of his purity and holiness.
Moses told the assembled people what he had heard from God, both the Ten Commandments and the Law (ch. 20-23), and the people declared their submission and readiness to obey God's commands.

Moses wrote the Ten Commandments and the Law as much as he remembered by God's grace, and afterward he received the Ten Commandments written by God's hand on two tablets; and to express his thanks to God he built an altar below the mountain and twelve pillars around it representing the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, to declare that the salvation of all the people depends on the sacrifice offered, which signifies the crucified Christ.
Burnt offerings: sacrifices that are burned entirely on the altar to please God.

Peace offerings: sacrifices that are slaughtered and a part of them is offered on the altar, and the people eat of the rest. Moses commanded some young men to offer sacrifices of oxen to God in thanks for His commandments that He had given them, since the tribe of Levi had not yet been set apart for service nor Aaron for the priesthood.

Use your time in the days of your youth and in the time when you are able to offer God worship, for there may come times when your body weakens or the cares of life hinder you; and your store of spiritual work will remind you of God and bring you back to Him, so that you meditate on and repeat the word of God that you lived with Him earlier, and enjoy it all your days. And the days of youth are not only at a certain age but in every time in which you are able to work, whatever your age, as long as God has given you strength to work.

When the oxen were slaughtered, Moses commanded, and they gathered the blood in basins, that is, wide vessels, in which he put half of the blood; and the other half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar, declaring that this is the blood with which God is pleased with them, and it signifies the blood of Christ the Redeemer.
The book of the covenant: God's commandments and His law are a covenant between Him and His people; if they keep them, He blesses them in all their life.
Moses read the commandments and the Law that he had written in a book, and when the people heard the word of God they confirmed again their readiness to obey Him.

Moses sprinkled the blood that was in the basins on the people to sanctify them by it, for it is a type of the blood of Christ the Savior, which we receive today in the sacraments of the Church; and he calls it the blood of the covenant because it is a covenant between God and His people: if they obey His commandments, He will be their God and will keep them and save them from all evil.
Moses carried out the word of God mentioned in (vv. 1, 2) and went up on the mountain, and he and Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and the seventy elders drew near to the foot of the mountain.
As it were the body of heaven: like heaven itself.

When they drew near the mountain, God appeared upon it in a form that was perhaps the form of a man, and under His feet they saw something great that they could not define, so they said of it that it was "a likeness of a work", that is, something made by the hand of God; it resembles a cloud, but its color is light blue and pure like the transparent blue sapphire, which is one of the precious, costly stones, and its color was the color of the pure sky. It may have appeared as a great light or some awesome sight, with beneath it a work of sapphire. The meaning of this is that God made something of His glory and splendor appear, but of course they did not see God Himself, as He said, "No man shall see Me and live" (Ezek 33:20).
The nobles of the children of Israel: Aaron and his sons and the elders of the people.

And everyone who comes near the holy mountain dies, because of the greatness of God, but "He laid not His hand", that is, He did not harm the people when they drew near the mountain, because it was God who sanctified them and cared for them.

And they all rejoiced at seeing God, and to express their joy they sat down to eat of the food they had taken with them, which was the peace offerings that the young men offered by the hand of Moses (v. 5).

When you enjoy seeing God in your prayers and meditations, your life is turned into a blessing, and you are able to do everything in holiness, whether eating or drinking or sleeping or recreation, for all things are pure to the pure.

God commanded Moses to come forward and go up the mountain so that He might give him the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone, and also the Law that God Himself wrote. For although Moses wrote the commandments and the Law after he came down from the mountain, God writes them for him Himself, lest anything of them should have fallen from him by oversight.
The mount of God: this is Mount Sinai.

Moses went forward, going up the mountain, and Joshua, his special disciple, followed him; for Moses was careful to disciple others such as Joshua, and also the leaders, the elders of Israel, to lead the people, especially since Joshua needed special discipling because he would lead the people after Moses.

Take care to give everything you know to others and disciple them so that they too may give, and so on...; so do not be selfish but concerned to teach everyone, not only through yourself but also through those whom you have discipled.

As for the seventy elders, he said to them that it was enough for them to come near to the foot of the mountain and see God in the form of sapphire. And before he bade them farewell, he said to them that if a dispute arises among you in anything, return to Aaron and Hur, who was also a disciple of Moses and used to support his hand when he prayed so that they might overcome Amalek (ch. 17:12); he was the grandfather of Bezaleel, who led the workers in setting up and making the tabernacle of the congregation (ch. 35:30, 31), and some Bible scholars consider him to have been the husband of Miriam, the sister of Moses. And the seventy elders judge the children of Israel in their various cases.

Moses went forward with his disciple Joshua to go up the mountain, and here they saw the mountain covered with a cloud as a sign of the presence of God, because the cloud points to heaven, for God is exalted above our minds and thoughts. This cloud remained covering the mountain for six days, and whenever Moses and Joshua lifted their eyes they found a thick cloud covering the mountain. God left them for this period so that they might feel the fear of Him, and after six days God called Moses to enter into the midst of the cloud.
The top of the mountain appeared as if covered with fire above the cloud, also declaring the presence of God, who is a consuming fire that crushes all evil.
And all the people of Israel saw this wonderful sight from afar so that they might fear God and be sanctified.

Moses left Joshua his disciple in the middle of the mountain and went up toward the summit and disappeared in the midst of the cloud to meet God and remain with Him forty days, enjoying conversation with Him in them, learning from Him the pattern of the tabernacle of the congregation and receiving the tablets of the commandment and the Law; that is, this time he did not go up for a short period as in the previous times but remained 40 days. He went up again and remained another 40 days (Ex 34:28) to receive the tablets of the Law after the breaking of the first two tablets. His fasting was by divine help, because an ordinary person cannot endure fasting 40 days, and so Elijah also fasted by the help of God (1 Kgs 19:11); and these two were a type of the fasting of Christ for us forty days and forty nights (Mt 3).
